en: *Jingjie Pinglin*, Volume One (Upper). Compiled by Jiao Hong, Ruohou, Father of the Grand Scribe Yiyuan,
for the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-bodhimaṇḍala-parivarta-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata, the Definitive Meaning).
Taishi Ruo-gang, Chen Yidian, Meng Changfu, Proofread. (Chao Wen-yuan said:

"At the beginning of the *Yuanjue jing*, the Buddha, for the sake of the twelve great beings, expounds the fundamental causes and virtues of the Tathāgata. One cultivates this through the three contemplations of *yuanjue*; this is essentially the process of attaining illumination from sincerity. (Shan-shan said: This... *Note:

The provided text fragment contains a portion of a preface or colophon regarding the *Yuanjue jing* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra). The parenthetical remarks by Chao Wen-yuan and Shan-shan discuss the soteriological structure of the sutra—specifically the movement from inherent sincerity (*cheng*) to manifest wisdom (*ming*) via the cultivation of the three contemplations.*
Awakening possesses the meaning of vastness and the meaning of squareness and roundness. This means that its essence is great while its function is broad;
its principle is square while its significance is round. "Square" signifies uprightness—neither biased nor deviant. "Round" signifies fulfillment—without deficiency or lack.

Furthermore, the "great square" may be taken as the essence, while the "broad roundness" is the function; this means the essence is great, square, and impartial, while the function is broad, perfect, and complete.

Because it is deficient [in those qualities]. Furthermore, "square" (fang) is used to connect with "greatness" (da), and "round" (yuan) is used to connect with "extensiveness" (guang). Moreover, the preceding three characters are specific, while the character "round" is general;
the intent is to clarify that this awakening is named "round" because it is fully endowed with the virtues of the three great natures.
Pei Xiu said: "Great" (da) refers to its nature being vast and expansive, like empty space. "Square" (fang) is named according to the dharmas;

its meaning is that of providing a standard and maintaining stability. It provides a standard that gives rise to understanding and maintains its own intrinsic nature. "Broad" (guang) is named according to its function; its meaning is extensive and manifold.
This "extensiveness and manifoldness" refers to this nature of Perfect Enlightenment, which inherently possesses wondrous qualities exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
Its function manifests secretly and responds subtly, without ceasing and without end.

That which is vast and expansive—this inexhaustible function—is such that each and every instance is identical to the enlightened nature (*bodhicit*), being without boundaries and without limitations. This is Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
This directly points to the essence of the Dharma. If one does not grasp the essence, then pointing at it is of no avail;

one would not know what "great" Dharma was spoken of before, nor what "vast" Dharma was taught. "Perfect" (yuan) means complete and all-encompassing; beyond this, there is not a single further dharma.

"Awakened" (jue) means empty, luminous, and spiritually radiant, devoid of all discriminative thoughts and conceptions. This awakening is neither separate from the mundane nor confined to the sagely; it is not apart from objects.
The mind is localized; yet the objects of the mind, whether mundane or sagely, are fundamentally empty, being nothing other than numinous awareness.

Therefore, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*). The three characters *sūtra* collectively refer to all the scriptures. The two characters "definitive meaning" (*liao-yi*) praise this single volume as the definitive meaning of all the scriptures.
Thus, the text below states: "This is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures. This is the first [section] of the scripture.
This is precisely this scripture. Now, for the sake of convenience in following the text, it is divided into three sections, balancing the detailed and the concise:

first, the time and the principal figures who heard with faith; second, the place of teaching based on reality; third, the assembly of dharmas of identical essence. Now, regarding the first: the time and the principal figures who heard with faith.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān entered the Great Treasury of Radiance of the Supernatural Powers.
(Zongmi said: When the Sage preaches the Dharma, he does so only to manifest the Tathatā (Suchness). Since only Suchness is "thus," it is called "Thus" (*evam*).

Furthermore, because the True does not contradict the Conventional, it is called "Such" (*tathā*); because the Conventional accords with the True, it is called "Thus" (*evam*). Moreover, "Such" refers to words that accord with principle, while "Thus" [refers to]...

There is no designation that is not non-erroneous. Furthermore, the non-duality of existence and non-existence constitutes suchness (*tathatā*). Suchness is neither existence nor non-existence; this is what is correct.
If we speak solely according to the present sutra, the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages are no different from the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*);

it is only these causes and effects that are free from error and are thus correct. (Zongmi said: "The Buddhas possess constant radiance and emit light. If we refer to this constant radiance, then...")
The *Tathāgatagarbha-śāstra* states: "When the nature of the mind does not arise, it is the great wisdom-light that universally illumines the dharma-realm.
If one considers the light emitted and the supernormal powers manifested, this is the treasury of the light of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-prabhā-garbha*)."
Mount Shāna said: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha; thus is the perfection of hearing. I am Mañjuśrī and Ānanda-sāgara.

As for these provisional designations of the five aggregates, how can they be called 'I'? There are four kinds of 'I': first, the pervasive conceptualization of ordinary beings; second, the sectarian tenets of non-Buddhists;
third, the provisional distinction of host and guest according to worldly convention among the various sages; and fourth, the Dharmakāya."

The "True Self" (ātman) refers here to the latter two [of the five aggregates]. Therefore, it is said that because [the self] does not exist, [it is called "I"]. "Hearing" means the arising of consciousness through the faculty of the ear;
although it depends upon the sense-base of the ear, one sets aside the specific [base] to follow the general [term], hence it is called "I heard. This is spoken without a mind of false pride.

According to the school of Non-characteristics (Nirākāravāda), since the self is already non-existent, hearing is also non-hearing, for all things are empty due to their dependence on conditions. Yet, this does not destroy conventional designations (prajñapti). That is to say:
"Not hearing what is heard" refers to the accomplishment of time. "At one time" means the moment of speaking and listening;
at this time, mind and object vanish, principle and wisdom merge, ordinary and sage are as one, and the original and the initial meet. This is the time when all these dualistic dharmas are one.
*Bhagavān* refers to the accomplishment of the Lord. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "One who can destroy the afflictions is called *Bhagavān*. This corresponds to the stage of severance.
Virtue manifests the Dharmakāya; when preaching the sutras in the Pure Land, the Dharma-body and Reward-body are not distinguished, for this is not a mere transformation body.
Thus, the *Buddhaguṇa Sūtra* states: "This Bhagavān is the most pure awakening, reaching the furthest limits of the Dharma-realm and exhausting the entirety of empty space."
Extending to the limits of the future. If we refer to various sutras, this is mostly the character "Buddha" (佛).孤山 (Gushan) said:

"The 'Treasury' (藏) refers to the *dharmadhātu-garbha* (the matrix of the dharma-realm), which is the *tathatā* (suchness) that gives rise to faith. This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and sentient beings, the essential nature of spiritual powers and radiant light.
The myriad virtues and functions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all contained within it; hundreds of thousands of penetrations and lights all proceed from this."
Because it arises [from within], it is called a "treasury" (garbha). It is also termed the Dharma-nature Land (dharmatā-bhūmi) and the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light.
To cease all conceptual discrimination so that wisdom merges with principle is what is meant by "entering."
Samādhi and right reception (*samyaksamādhi*). It is the majestic abiding maintained by the light of all Tathāgatas; it is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings. (As Master Shan said:

"Samādhi and right reception" refers to what is stated in the treatise: that outflows (*anāsrava*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the various illusory manifestations of karma are all identical in their essence and characteristics to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without difference.")

[Distinction]. (The Treatise says: "All sentient beings are fundamentally and eternally abiding, having entered into nirvana. However, when the sages realize this realm, they simply call it 'abiding and maintaining' [zhuchi];
ordinary people do not know they are the same, but merely point to 'awakening' [jue]. )
Zongmi said: "This indicates both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms. Abiding securely within the treasury [of the mind], not receiving any further sensations, is called *samāpatti* (correct reception).
Furthermore, *samādhi* is translated here as 'correct contemplation,' meaning that while in meditative concentration, one carefully and correctly examines the object of focus.
Second, regarding the identity of essence with ordinary beings and sages: once one has entered its source, one is identical to its essence."

The luminosity of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna) is suchness; the luminosity of initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi) comes forth. When the initial and the original are non-dual, it is called the Tathāgata.
Thus, sentient beings possess the original [enlightenment] but lack the initial [awakening]; this suchness does not come.

As the Mountain says: "Layer upon layer, the interlacing lights shine forth with brilliant clarity; this is called 'Radiant Adornment' (*Prabhāsa-vyūha*). To dwell securely, forever severing all攀缘 (*ālambana*, objective conditions), is called 'Dwelling' (*Vihāra*).

To maintain this without loss or decay is called 'Sustaining' (*Dhṛti*). Regarding the phrase "these various [beings] below": they are deluded regarding the Truth and give rise to falsehood, thus falsely perceiving sentient beings.
Yet the essence of falsehood is fundamentally empty; it is entirely the ground of the originally awakened mind (*mūla-bodhicitta*). Since falsehood cannot defile it, it is so stated.
Because of purity, body and mind are quiescent, reaching the state of equality at the primordial limit (Pei Xiu said:
"All are of one and the same limit; this is the primordial limit of Perfect Enlightenment").

Mount Shan said: "The bodies and minds of ordinary beings and sages are alike in that their appearances—whether perceived as similar or different—are all empty and false. In their very essence, they are quiescent;
because they are quiescent, they are equal."
It is perfected throughout the ten directions, in accord with non-duality.
(Zongmi says: "In accord with non-duality" means to accord with that which is non-dual. This is because the Western language is inverted;
the translators did not fully reverse the phrasing.)
Mount Shān said: "Since it is no different from the essence of awakening, it is perfect and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm according to that essence.
Birth-and-death and nirvana constitute a duality; ordinary beings follow birth-and-death, while those of the Two Vehicles head toward nirvana. Now, we abide in neither."

Therefore, it is said that one "accords with" [reality]. Furthermore, regarding the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), purity and impurity are non-dual; regarding the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*), sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual;
regarding the essential substance, body and mind are non-dual; and regarding universal inclusion, self and others are non-dual. To be in resonance with this is what constitutes "accordance."
Within the non-dual realm, all pure lands are manifested. (Pei Xiu said:
Although there are many lands, they do not exceed three types: first, the Dharma-nature land; second, the Enjoyment land; third, the Transformation land.

If one distinguishes between self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment within the Enjoyment land, they become four lands. As for their conditions, there are only two kinds: namely, the pure and the defiled—or alternatively, essence and appearance.)
Zongmi said: "The Buddha has no thought of manifesting lands; yet, like a clear mirror that is without mind, he manifests all pure lands.
This is responding to conditions through non-thought, just as a clear mirror manifests images without mind. Thus, Master Zhao said:"
Pure lands and defiled lands are established according to what is appropriate for sentient beings. To those who prefer purity, one shows precious jewels;

to those who prefer defilement, one shows tiles and rubble. Beauty and ugliness originate with them; they have no fixed nature within me. A land that has no fixed nature is precisely what is called a "pure land.
Because it universally responds to all types of beings, it is said to be "various" (*zhū*).
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Their names were:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva, Vaśavartin-tejas Bodhisattva, Ghoṣavyāhāra Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva, and Samantabodhi.
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, the Bodhisattva Chief of the Virtuous and Good, and others as their leaders, together with their retinues,
all entered into samādhi and dwelt together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.
Pei Xiu said: "Bodhi" is translated here as "Awakening," which refers to the fruit of Buddhahood sought; "Sattva" is translated as "sentient beings," which refers to the beings to be transformed.
Furthermore, this [term] implies an awakening that possesses clear realization, as opposed to the emotional states of discursive thought;
it thus refers to sentient beings who seek Bodhi. "Mahā" means "great. Although ten thousand people are mentioned, the text specifically enumerates only the various Bodhisattvas.
[He was] the leader of one hundred thousand [beings].
As for the statement "all entered samādhi," it is because by entering meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), they attained the realm of the Buddha.

At that time, the bodies of ordinary beings and sages were identical, for cause and effect shared a single characteristic. Thus, what is called a "Dharma assembly" is an assembly of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
There is neither self nor person. From this point onward, within the section on the orthodox teaching (*zhengzongfen*), the eleven rounds of question and answer are condensed into two parts.

The first round of question and answer causes one to believe and understand the true reality, thereby fulfilling the original cause for arising [in the path]. The subsequent ten rounds of question and answer cause one to practice in accordance with that understanding, entering realization according to one's faculties.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, we pray that you will, for the sake of all the members of the Dharma assembly who have gathered here, expound upon the Tathāgata’s primordial arising in purity."

This is the practice of the Dharma according to the stages. Furthermore, it explains how a bodhisattva, having generated a pure mind within the Mahāyāna, remains free from all afflictions and illnesses, thereby enabling sentient beings of future末 (mò) times who seek the Mahāyāna not to fall into false views.
(Zongmi said: "Mañjuśrī" is translated here as "Wondrous Head" (*Miaoshou*) and also as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*).
It represents the wisdom of faith and understanding. It is also called "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*), representing realized wisdom.

In this text, the fundamental stage of the causal ground is explained, investigating the ultimate reality and its delusions in order to establish correct understanding and perfect the faculty of faith. (Zongmi said: "Those who seek the Mahāyāna," etc., means...)

In the age of the Final Dharma, right understanding is difficult to attain. Those who indulge their minds in the five desires, those who follow and practice heterodox paths, or those who are attached to the two vehicles—these are set aside as being beyond the scope of this teaching.
Even if there are those who have resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna, if they do not hear this Dharma-gate, they will likewise fall into false views.
Mount Shān said: "The Buddha’s original mind, which first arose from the fundamental source, perfectly illumines the essential body (dharmatā) and is inherently free from afflictions;
therefore, it is called 'originally arisen purity. As for 'the virtues and practices that serve as causes,' these refer to the virtues of the mind upon which those practices depend.
The essence of the Mahāyāna is this fundamental and initial awakening (mūla-ādi-bodhi). Now, please explain its manifestation within the awakened mind."
Regarding "the mind": "one who gives rise to a pure mind" refers to the second arousal of the bodhicitta mentioned previously.
Once this mind has been aroused, it is never again forgotten. Because it is not forgotten, one is not disturbed by the delusions of Māra;
therefore, he requests that the single flavor of definitive truth be proclaimed, so that those seeking the Mahāyāna, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, shall not fall into wrong views.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

It is well that you have been able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the dharmic practices of the stages of the ground for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age who seek the Mahāyāna, so that they may attain correct maintenance and not fall into false views. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake."
"Good son, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
From it flow forth all that is pure: true thusness (*tathatā*), bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the *pāramitās*, which are taught to the bodhisattvas.
The original ground of practice for all Tathāgatas relies entirely upon the aspect of perfectly illuminating, pure awakening; only by forever severing ignorance do they attain Buddhahood."

The Path. What is ignorance? (The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* commentary states: "To say 'Excellent' twice signifies the ultimate excellence. The definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna ought to be proclaimed;

yet, as the needle and the magnet have not yet met, one must remain silent regarding this essential point for the time being. Now that we have encountered this auspicious assembly, where those with mature faculties have all arrived, I shall expound the subtle [Dharma]. )

"An entrance must necessarily rely upon the posing of questions; what you have requested now truly serves to inspire me. The benefit and joy [therein] are indeed great; I speak again to praise this as excellent.
To seek anything apart from the fundamental mind, whether perceiving it as false or perceiving it as true, constitutes dualistic and erroneous views.
(Pei Xiu said: "The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally non-existent; that which undergoes illusory transformation is precisely Suchness (*tathatā*). 'True' means reality.")
This reveals that it is not false or illusory. "Suchness" (tathatā) means being as it is; it signifies the absence of change.

This refers to the ultimate reality, which remains eternally according to its own nature across all states. Furthermore, "true" (zhen) means its essence is not deceptive or false, and "as" (ru) means its nature is without alteration.
Therefore, it is called True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*). (Zongmi said: "Flowing forth" does not mean that there is a separate dharma flowing out from within to the outside; rather...)
Based on the nature of awakening, it manifests various gateways; its virtues are inexhaustible, and its application is tireless, which is why it is called "flowing forth."

Mount Shou said: "The World-Honored One first praised and then granted permission; that he further commands you to 'listen attentively' is truly to ensure that you examine with precision and do not allow other conditions to intermingle.
Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to listen to the Dharma of the true mark. [He is] the Unsurpassed Dharma King."
The Buddha is one who possesses mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*), and there is nothing superior to him. *Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*).

This means that within the essence of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), there are virtues and functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from the very beginning, these have been maintained without loss.
"Gate" (*mukha*) carries the meaning of "entry and exit. "Perfect enlightenment" directly refers to the essence of the Dharma. From within it, all that is pure flows forth.
*Tathatā* (True Suchness); *bodhi*, here translated as "awakening" (*jue*); *nirvāṇa*, here translated as "quiescent extinction" (*jimiè*);
*pāra*, here translated as "the other shore. *Mitra* is the transliteration for *mitra*; it should be rendered as "reaching the other shore.

"Instructing the Bodhisattvas" reveals the functional activity of the dharmas such as True Suchness that flow forth from above. The Bodhisattvas are those who are instructed; True Suchness and the others are that which instructs.

Therefore, it is said that True Suchness (Tathatā) is the principle. The next two are the fruits, while the pāramitās are the causes—the ground upon which all Tathāgatas originally established their practice.
This restates what was asked. "All rely" means that there is no Buddha who does not do so. "Perfectly illuminating" refers to the illuminator;
being free from partiality and deviation, it is the aspect of pure awakening. "Silent, desolate, empty, and vast" refers to that which is illuminated.
When the insentient dusts are completely understood, the essence of illumination is likewise pure; this is the characteristic of awakening.

However, because one has only recently awakened and the subject-object duality has not yet been forgotten, it is called a "characteristic. Once fundamental awakening is manifested, ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and will ultimately never arise.
This is called "eternal severance. Countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges take this as their cause.

However, if one wishes to clarify the pure nature of awakening and reveal the wondrous gate of the Perfect and Sudden, and does not first investigate and shatter ignorance, then all that is done merely supports delusion.
Therefore, by resolving that the true mind is inherently existent and that the false nature is fundamentally non-existent, and by relying on this clear realization, one finally attains it.
This is called the virtue of the cause. Therefore, he inquires: "What is ignorance?
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions, like a person who has lost their way and confuses the four directions."

(Shan said: "Inversion" refers to having attachments; "madness" refers merely to being wild and frantic. Because of madness, there is inversion—just as by losing one's way, one mistakenly identifies another direction as home.
Zongmi said: "Sentient beings have never attained awakening, and thus their mental consciousnesses are deranged and chaotic. They turn their backs on enlightenment and unite with the sensory dusts.
It is like a person who, suddenly arriving at a riverbank or entering a desolate wilderness, becomes bewildered and mistakes east for west. Once one direction is..."
When deluded, the other three [mental factors] operate simultaneously; hence it is called a "changeable state. However, at the very moment of being deluded, the fundamental direction does not change;
when one suddenly awakens, it is still the original direction.
They falsely recognize the four elements as the characteristics of their own bodies, and the shadows of conditions from the six sense-objects as the characteristics of their own minds.
This is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky or a second moon. Good son, in reality there are no flowers in the sky; it is only the sick person who grasps at them as real.
(Fei Xiu said: "Delusion regarding the body and delusion regarding the mind comprise four pairs in total.
To mistake the four great elements—which are not the self—for the self, while failing to recognize the Dharma-body as the true self, constitutes the first pair.

To perceive the four great elements—which are illusory and fundamentally non-existent—as existent, while perceiving the Dharma-body—which is real and fundamentally existent—as non-existent, constitutes the second pair. To take conditioned thoughts and arising-extinguishing phenomena as..."
The true mind. The true mind is luminously clear, yet one does not recognize it oneself; this is the third pair. Contingent thoughts are like the black speck within a pearl:

they are entirely empty, yet one clings to them as existent. The true mind is like the luminous quality within the pearl: it is truly existent, yet one perceives it as non-existent; this is the fourth pair.
Mount Shan said: "The four great elements exist through the provisional conjunction of conditions; they are without self and without master, being ultimately empty.
They are devoid of 'I' and 'mine. That ordinary beings perform various karmas and transmigrate through the long kalpas is solely due to their delusion regarding their own *dharmakāya*.
They grasp these four great elements as the self, the six sense objects as the environment, and the essence of consciousness as the mind. Thus, the mind confronts the sense organs and their objects."

There is the appearance of objective conditions (*ālambana*). These appearances are like shadows; in their entirety, they are utterly non-existent. The luminous clarity of one’s own mind is fundamentally not an object of conceptualization (*ālambana*).
Yet, now one identifies these objects of conceptualization as one's own mind, following after them moment by moment, drifting and sinking in the ocean of suffering.

It is like a pearl that is transparent and clear, which is fundamentally neither blue nor yellow; yet when it encounters blue or yellow, a shadow-like appearance arises. The fool clings to its color and [mistakes it for the jewel itself].

This is that very pearl. It is like mistaking the reflections of conditions for one's own mind. For example, it is like an eye afflicted with cataracts looking into the sky and falsely seeing flowers where there are none;
or like pressing the eyes while gazing at the lunar disc and seeing a separate moon beside it. These "flowers in the sky" and the "illusory moon" are all metaphors for false perception.
When sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, become deluded and their minds are as eyes afflicted with cataracts, they falsely perceive [distinctions] within the perfectly luminous essence.

Because the body and mind arise and perish, it is said that in reality there are no flowers. The phrase "the patient’s false attachment" directly addresses the previous statement regarding false recognition.
If one awakens to the fact that True Suchness is signless and is but the One Mind, then it is like space, which fundamentally has no flowers.
In the heavens there is but one moon;
yet due to false attachment, they are not only deluded regarding the self-nature of this empty space, but are also confused as to the actual source from which the flowers arise.
Because of this, they falsely undergo the cycle of birth and death; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

(Shouleng says: "Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-faculties are removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfectly pure.
(Zongmi says: "It is not only that one is deluded regarding this empty space. From these two lines onward, if one were to provide the full correspondence with the Dharma, it should say:
'Not only is one deluded regarding the self-nature of this true emptiness, but one is also confused about the place where that body and mind arise.'"")
Mount Shān said: "The nature of empty space is pure and devoid of things. Now, by grasping at flowers as arising within emptiness, it is as if emptiness itself has transformed into flowers.
To falsely perceive 'flowers in the sky'—arising where there is no arising, forming things where there are no things—is to delude oneself regarding the nature of empty space.
Since you grasp that the flowers arise from emptiness, you fail to realize they arise from a cataract in the eye. Regarding the cataract:

Thus, it is truly the place where flowers arise, not that there are actual flowers. This is merely to marvel at how flowers exist within the void, while failing to realize that there is a film over the eyes.
Outwardly one laments the suffering and affliction of body and mind, yet does not know that this stems from harboring deluded sentiments and falsely clinging to body and mind.
Consequently, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one revolves in saṃsāra without end, [passing through] the eight [hot hells].

The five types of decay are suffering; because their harm is so profound, they are called ignorance (*avidyā*). Wisdom (*vidyā*) causes people to attain liberation and not be born into the cycle of rebirth.
Good son, this ignorance has no real substance; it is like a person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet...
Upon waking, there was nothing at all to be found. (As Shan said:
"It is only this ignorance that arises crosswise from emptiness. Now I have realized that when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease;

when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; and so on, until old age and death cease. (He further said: "Having realized that this has no substance, all conditioned phenomena [saṃskāra] do not..."
"Arising. Because there is no arising, there is no cessation. When arising and cessation have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss.
Pei Xiu said: "This name 'ignorance' is merely a provisional designation. Whether sought internally or externally, it is utterly unfindable.
When its limits are investigated, it is fundamentally wondrous clarity; therefore, it is said that it has no real substance. Since it is said to have no substance, the Way..."
The principle is difficult to perceive. It is like objects seen in a dream while sleeping; one simply perceives them as existing, yet upon waking and seeking them, they can never be found.
It is like various empty flowers vanishing into space; one cannot say that there is a specific place where they were extinguished. Why? Because they are non-existent.
Because of the locus of birth, all sentient beings falsely perceive arising and ceasing within that which is non-arising; therefore, it is called the cycle of birth and death.
(The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "This delusion has no root; its nature is ultimately empty. Originally there was no delusion, yet there appears to be the awareness of delusion.")
Awakening to delusion causes delusion to cease; when awakening does not give rise to delusion, this is precisely the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If one can decisively accept this within the mind, it is called the Dharma of Non-arising. As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "All dharmas are without arising; all dharmas are without cessation.
If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas are ever present before one."
Zongmi said: "If empty flowers had no place of extinction, they would surely return; for what reason, then, do you say they are 'empty and non-existent'?
It is because when they were seen, they originally had no place of arising; since they were not seen, how could one seek a place of extinction?
It was previously stated that birth and death arise from ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, how can there be birth and death? Ignorance and birth and death are, from the beginning..."
In the end, everything is utterly non-existent. Within this non-existence, sentient beings, through their deluded minds, perversely perceive birth and death.
Because of these perverse perceptions, it is called "revolving in birth and death."

Good son, when a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, he knows these to be like flowers in the sky; thus there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death.
It is not that they are absent because of some deliberate effort, but because they are non-existent by their very nature.
(Zongmi said: "The empty flowers [are] themselves the absence of saṃsāra. A single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold;
a single word of ultimate truth transforms the ordinary person into a sage. (Fei Xiu said: "If one calculates that there is a body and mind, one has not yet escaped saṃsāra;
this is because one has not yet abandoned the attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*). If there is neither body nor mind, then 'self' and 'what belongs to self' perish, and only then is there liberation.")
This is to illuminate the emptiness of the five aggregates and to deliver one from all calamities (is □□□□□□).
As it says in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "One who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment knows these to be like flowers in the sky; this is to awaken to delusion by relying upon the True."
Since one knows that all phenomena are like flowers in the sky, how could one further perceive the existence of saṃsāra? This is the dharma of neither birth nor death.
Not only is there no such dharma, but there is also no person who undergoes birth and death. Externally, one leaves behind the world; internally, one is liberated from body and mind.
One does not calculate the body; the body is identical to empty space. One does not calculate the mind; the mind is identical to the *dharmadhātu*.

Yet, this emptiness and non-existence of body and mind is not attained through the practice of contemplation by means of a self. Their nature is primordially empty and quiescent because they have never existed from the beginning.
Thus, the *Vajra-tri-kāla-sūtra* says: "If these sentient beings are unborn within transformation, and do not give rise to non-transformation, that transformation is great."
Next, by successively wiping away these traces, one explains the establishment of the true cause.
That which perceives is like empty space; that which perceives empty space is itself a mark of a flower in the sky. Yet, one cannot say that the nature of perception is non-existent.
When both existence and non-existence are discarded, this is called "pure awakening in accordance with reality."
(Xing explains: "This section has four points: first, it subverts the wisdom that perceives delusion; second, it further dissolves the mind that subverts;
third, it precludes the view of annihilation; fourth, it provides a summary. Regarding its departure from the past and future, it explains the causes and conditions [of this process].
The subsequent text then investigates the reasons for the subversion and returns to the ultimate reality)."
Mount Shan said: "That which is aware is able to realize that the nature of body and mind is fundamentally non-existent, just as the great void contains nothing at all.
To know that this 'ability to be aware' is non-existent is itself like a flower in the sky; thus, the fault is non-existent. Furthermore, one cannot say there is no nature of awareness;
it is simply that thoughts do not arise to discriminate between emptiness and existence. Since both existence and non-existence are inappropriate,"
Sentimentality is precisely the severance of the path of mind and speech; the essence of pure awakening is thereby manifested.
To simply not turn one's back on it while engaging with sensory objects is what is called "conformity. Nor is there anything else that can conform to it; thus, Kumārajīva said:
"To have no mind regarding engagement—this is true engagement. Because one conforms to pure awakening, it is called "pure awakening is conformed to. In this way, all grasping is exhausted.

Once the illness has been removed, one may then arouse the mind to practice; thus, even gathering sand or drawing on the ground, joining the palms, or bowing the head—all these lead to the attainment of the Buddha-way.
To cultivate in this manner may be called the "True Cause."

Why is this? Because it is the nature of empty space; because it is eternally unmoving; because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is neither arising nor ceasing; because it is devoid of cognition or vision;

and because, like the nature of the Dharmadhātu, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions. This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
By means of this, Bodhisattvas give rise to the pure mind within the Mahāyāna. Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age should rely upon this.
This practice does not fall into false views. (Pei Xiu said:
"The two phrases 'the nature of space is eternally unmoving' clarify all dharmas; these do not all manifest the single mind.
The Treatise points to the single mind by calling it the *tathāgatagarbha*. The *Laṅkāvatāra* also says: 'That which is quiescent and extinguished is called...')"
"One mind. One mind is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. (Zongmi says: "Without arising or ceasing, without knowing or seeing;
it is not only that it cannot be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), but it is also that it cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*).

When both consciousness and wisdom are identical to suchness (*tathatā*), only then is it the self-substance, the true cognition, the great wisdom-light that shines everywhere. (Zongmi says: "The nature of the *dharmadhātu* and the *tathāgata*...")
The "store" (garbha) is identical in essence but distinct in meaning, and there are two such distinctions: first, when it is among the category of sentient beings, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*;
when it is among the category of insentient things, it is called the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Mount Shān said: "The body and mind are illusory and false; they may be described as entirely empty. Awareness accords with principle—why, then, do you negate it?
When both existence and non-existence are transcended, upon what basis can one practice? Indeed, all phenomena arise from conditions and are like space;
they are fundamentally unarisen and now cannot be extinguished. It is not that they become entirely empty only through negation. Furthermore, regarding all dharmas..."
It is eternally quiescent and immovable; it neither comes nor goes. It is not that which has already passed, nor that which is yet to come, nor that which arises in the present.
Therefore, within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no arising or ceasing, and no cognition or vision. Indeed, to perceive the arising of birth and death is what is called clinging to deluded sentiments.
To perceive the cessation of birth and death is what is called "awareness. Now, since there is nothing that can arise or cease, how could there be a subject that grasps or a faculty that knows?
Sentient beings and their environment interpenetrate; mind and objects are not divided. The storehouse consciousness is like the nature of the Dharma-realm;

investigating the three periods of time, it remains eternally as it is from beginning to end. Pervading all of space, it is replete with all virtues, perfectly complete and omnipresent throughout the ten directions.
It is boundless and limitless because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is inherently such from the beginning.
Why should one diminish the old or add to the new, or extinguish delusions to give rise to wisdom? Therefore, by dissolving these three layers [of duality], one merges darkly with the awakened mind.

Taking this as the foundation for practice, one first attains the true name of a Bodhisattva on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*). The following section merely concludes the preceding text and contains no further distinct meaning.
Thereupon, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, for the sake of this assembly of bodhisattvas, and for all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate the Mahāyāna, having heard of this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment, how should they practice? World-Honored One, if those sentient beings..."
One who knows that things are like illusions finds that body and mind are likewise illusory. How can one use an illusion to cultivate an illusion?
If the nature of all illusions were entirely extinguished, there would be no mind; who then would be the one to practice? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion?

If all sentient beings have not originally practiced cultivation, they will constantly dwell within birth and death as mere illusions and transformations, never understanding that their realm is like an illusion.
How can they liberate their deluded minds? I pray that you will act for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age.
By what skillful means should one gradually practice so as to cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind all illusions?

(Zongmi says: There are briefly three explanations for the meaning of Samantabhadra (*Puxian*). First, regarding its essential nature: its substance is all-pervasive, hence it is called "Universal" (*Samanta*);

it accomplishes virtues in accordance with conditions, hence it is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*). Second, regarding the various stages: it provides salvation through winding paths without deviation, hence it is called "Universal"; it is adjacent to the ultimate yet slightly inferior [to it]...)

The Sage is called "Worthy" (xian). Third, because his virtues within his own station are all-encompassing, he is called "Universal" (pu). Being harmonious, supple, good, and compliant, he is called "Worthy. This represents the practice in accordance with principle.
Now, within this gate, based on the wondrous mind of *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature), one examines illusory phenomena to clarify right practice.

Pei Xiu said: "Regarding the text on 'like an illusion,' both the phenomena (*dharma*) and the metaphors (*upamā*) each open up five points. Within the metaphors, there are five; for example, it is like tying a single [knot]."

[In the center: A horse created by illusion. [Regarding the five points within the central basis: First, the magician’s artifice; second, the illusory horse; third, the horse’s existence as it is, which is non-existent;

fourth, the deluded clinging to it as a horse; fifth, the true nature. Among these five factors: first, the true nature (*tathatā*); second, consciousness (*vijñāna*); third, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

fourth, the emptiness of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*); fifth, the deluded clinging to self and phenomena. All subsequent metaphors of illusion should be understood according to this pattern).
(Zongmi said: The passage in the sutra beginning with "If the nature of all illusions... follows from the previous section on "erasing traces.

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "The mind of sentient beings is by nature originally empty and quiescent. Since the essence of this empty and quiescent mind has no form or characteristics, how can one cultivate it to attain the original empty mind?")

Mount Shāna said: "To believe in and understand Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-bodhi) is to accord with one's own capacity. Although one may realize the heavenly truth (*t'ien-chên*), one has not yet clarified dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The Great Being, out of compassion, reaches down to receive those in the lower realms; he repeatedly questions them so that they may apply their minds to understanding and practice.

How do these harmonize? [The text continues: 'The World-Honored One [said]: He who knows that all is like an illusion realizes that body and mind are also illusory—this is understanding. How can one use the illusory to return [to the source]? "
"Cultivating illusion" refers to practice. This means that since both body and mind are already like an illusion, one is able to know that they are also illusory;
using illusion to eliminate illusion—how could there be any end to such illusion upon illusion? "If the nature of all illusions... and so forth, means:

if, because of being illusory, everything is empty and both subject and object are entirely non-existent, then who is there to perform cultivation? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion? If...

All sentient beings were originally empty and originally did not practice; thus they have produced much suffering in birth and death. Now they are empty and now do not practice; how then can they be liberated from suffering?
Those who do not understand that the realm of phenomena is like an illusion have not yet attained realization of the characteristics of dependent origination.
Having failed to realize the nature of things from the beginning, their deluded thoughts remain unliberated. If they still do not understand this now, how can they attain liberation?

Therefore, one may request instruction on the cultivation of skillful means. This means that although one initially contemplates the single essence and realizes it to be entirely true, later, when encountering the eight winds, delusions arise in confusion.

One’s practice is like that of a destitute son, and one’s understanding is like a flash of lightning. By what dharma can one cultivate and rectify this so as to forever eliminate the root of the ailment?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to cultivate the illusory samādhi of the bodhisattvas and its gradual stages of skillful means, so as to enable all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. Good son, all..."
The various illusory manifestations of sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just like flowers in the sky that appear from space.
Although the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space remains unimpaired.
(As Shan said: "The World-Honored One told Samantabhadra that, in brief, there are four points: first, he designates that illusion arises from [awakening] to serve as the fundamental principle;

second, he clarifies that when illusion is exhausted, awakening is fulfilled, thereby resolving the preceding doubts; third, he largely leaves illusion behind to reveal awakening, correctly demonstrating the application of the mind;
fourth, he distinguishes that illusion and awakening do not coexist, concluding by answering his request. (Zongmi said: "The false arises based upon the true.")

It is said that the Real (zhen) is the source. Yet, for the time being, one is deluded regarding the Real. The Real is fundamentally not mysterious; it is like two moons appearing based upon the single moon.
Relying on the single moon as their origin, although there is a basis for the "two," in reality there are no two orbs. Thus, these two have no substantial essence.
Therefore, the sutras state that various phenomena arise from the awakened mind (*buddhi-citta*); it is not that the mind gives rise to various phenomena.

Nevertheless, while both the sutras and śāstras universally teach that "the myriad dharmas are one mind" and "the three realms are consciousness-only," there are differences in their doctrinal lineages (*siddhānta-mārga*) that scholars rarely understand.

Zongmi said: "Samādhi" is translated here as "right reception" (zhèngshòu). Because one realizes that body and mind are like illusions, one merges with the original awakening of True Suchness (tathatā), just as a mirror receives reflections. It is called "right reception" because it neither accepts nor rejects.
The various illusory transformations refer to the contaminated five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements. All these pervasive phenomena are entirely non-existent.
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they must depend on a basis; they arise based upon the mind of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfected awakening).

To give rise to delusion based on the truth is like seeing flowers in the sky: ultimately, there is truly no arising or ceasing. It is merely due to cataracts in the eye that one sees flowers in the sky;
when the cataracts are present, the flowers appear in dependence upon the sky, and thus it is said they exist "from the sky. This is like the wondrous *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*.
The nature is ultimately without arising; it is only because the mind is deluded that one perceives delusion within the nature.
When deluded, delusion manifests based upon awakening; therefore, it is said to "arise from awakening. However, when there is an eye disease, one sees flowers arise in empty space;
when the disease is cured, one sees the flowers perish in empty space. Although the flowers perish, the emptiness remains constant. Yet, when the flowers arise, they do not...
When arising occurs, there is no extinction at the time of extinction. Because there is visual impairment and discrepancy, one perceives arising and perceives extinction.

The illusory mind of sentient beings returns to extinction by relying on illusion; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind is unmoving. It is based on illusion that awakening is described.
It is also called illusion. If one says there is awareness, one has not yet departed from illusion; if one says there is no awareness, it is likewise so.
Therefore, the cessation of illusion is called immovability.

(Regarding the section beginning with "This group of sentient beings": it states that the illusory extinction is vast and pervasive. Regarding the section beginning with "Relying on illusion": it joins with the following section to cause one to leave illusion behind and manifest awakening.

This is the formal instruction on the application of the mind, which directly answers the intent of the previous inquiry regarding practice. (Zongmi said: "In Samantabhadra’s question, there is no doubt as to whether one should practice or not;
rather, within the context of practice, there is doubt concerning the violation of the application of the mind. For the time being, [the answer] proceeds in a single direction... )
I only request: how should one practice to depart from illusion? Furthermore, this also preempts the fault of failing to practice. Thus, this section concludes the resolution of doubts.
It further demonstrates the application of the mind; the subsequent section will then harmonize the discourse on skillful means and gradual stages.
Mount Shān said: "This illusory mind is extinguished only through thorough understanding and penetration. That which is understood is illusion; that which understands is also illusion.

When both subject and object vanish, one accords with Perfect Enlightenment (Pūrṇabodhi). It is like waves arising from water: when the waves subside, the water remains. Illusion arises from enlightenment;
when illusion is extinguished, enlightenment is fulfilled. To speak of enlightenment based on illusion is merely to arise in response to conditions."
Therefore, this too is an illusion. If one speaks of "awakening," then awakening that is contrasted with delusion is also called an illusion;
however, awakening that is not contrasted with delusion—the primordial awakening—is not empty or illusory. If this mind arises, its arising is like an illusion.

If one claims that when a single awakening occurs, both [delusion and awakening] are absent, and thus it is called "real," this very notion is inherently like an illusion. To speak by way of change, [it] arises...
When the mind moves and thoughts arise, whether one speaks of the false or the true, there is nothing that is not illusion.

If all designations are extinguished and discrimination does not arise, the true mind of perfect enlightenment will manifest spontaneously. Since from the beginning there has been no illusory transformation, it is said to be "immovable."
"Good son, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they firmly maintain this mind of distancing, even that mind which is like an illusion is likewise distanced."

To distance oneself from illusion is itself a distancing; to distance oneself from that distancing of illusion is also a distancing. When there is nothing further to be distanced, all illusions are eliminated.
(Pei Xiu said: "There are two meanings to 'nothing further to be distanced. First, it is to merge with true awakening. True awakening..."
It cannot be separated from it. Once one reaches the midst of true awakening, there is naturally no longer any such illusion as described in the preceding section that can be discarded.
Therefore, Heze said: "When delusion arises, it is itself awakening; when delusion ceases, awakening ceases."
Mount Shān said: "To remain far removed from all illusory and false realms" means to distance oneself from all illusory objects.
"Because one firmly maintains this mind of distancing, even the mind that is like an illusion is likewise distanced" means to distance oneself from the very mind that distances itself from illusions.
"Distancing itself becomes an illusion, which is likewise distanced" means to distance oneself from the act of distancing itself from illusions.
One distances oneself from distancing itself, and further distances oneself from that distancing; this is the distancing of distancing. There are two aspects to what is called "distancing":

one is *śamatha* (calm abiding) and the other is *vipaśyanā* (insight). Regarding distancing through *śamatha*: it is the resting of the mind and the cessation of mental activity, never again pursuing or clinging to objects—like a person who, upon encountering a bear, should not attempt to confront it.
Regarding distancing through *vipaśyanā*: it is the realization that all phenomena are like space, their essential nature being empty, just as in a dream.
Regarding shackles and fetters: once awake, one has already left them behind. To see a dream within a dream is to successively realize the error of what preceded it;
only upon reaching the state of full awakening does what is seen become real. Therefore it is said: "When there is nothing to be separated from, all illusions are eliminated."
It is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood interact, fire emerges and the wood is consumed; the ashes fly away and the smoke vanishes.
Cultivating illusion with illusion is likewise so. Although all illusions are exhausted, one does not enter into annihilation.

(Below this, the non-coexistence of illusion and awakening is distinguished, concluding the response to the request. (Pei Xiu said: "In the analogy, the relationship between the earth and the manifestation of awakening was omitted for brevity.

If one wishes to provide it in full, one should use the earth as a metaphor for Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Wood arises from the earth; when it is burned away and completely exhausted, only the earth remains.
The mind arises through illusory transformation within Perfect Awakening; when the illusory transformations of the mind are dispelled and exhausted," [only Perfect Awakening remains].)
"Perfect Enlightenment is originally unmoving.
Zongmi said: "Suppose there is a piece of dry wood; when it is drilled with a wooden fire-drill, fire emerges and in turn burns both pieces of wood.
Once the wood and fire are exhausted, the smoke naturally ceases. Once extinguished, the ashes fly away spontaneously."
It disperses. This is not like the two pieces of wood, where their physical forms act as mutual obstructions. The wooden segments metaphorize the illusory and deluded objects of cultivation;
the fire-drill metaphorizes the illusory wisdom that performs the cultivation. The smoke metaphorizes separation; the ash metaphorizes elimination.
The three preceding lines—"cultivating the illusory with the illusory"—correspond precisely to the explicit text of the analogy. The final line additionally and implicitly reveals true awakening.
Good son, when one knows illusion, one is immediately detached from it; no expedient means need be employed. When one is detached from illusion, one is immediately awakened;
there is likewise no gradual progression. All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this will thus be able to forever leave behind all illusions.
(As previously stated: "By what means and through what gradual cultivation can all sentient beings be made to forever leave behind all illusions?

Thus, the Buddha has finished demonstrating the application of the mind and concludes his answer: "Without employing means and without gradual succession, it is in this way that one can forever leave behind all illusions.
This passage serves to synthesize and resolve the questions posed therein.)
Mount Shān said: "To know that this is an illusion is already called 'detachment. Once one has attained detachment from illusion, it is fundamentally awakening;
there are no further stages through which one gradually transforms into awakening. It is like a person who dreams of a wound on their body and seeks a physician for medicine;

once they have awakened and realized it was a dream, what further expedient means would they need to employ? If one waits for such expedients and practices them to gradually become detached, [one remains within the realm of duality]."
This is precisely the true dharma; why then is it called an illusion? If one clings to it as truly existent, that is still a false conceptualization; how then can it be called "cultivation"?
From the passage "All Bodhisattvas" below, the text concludes by establishing true detachment. This also serves as a general conclusion to the preceding section on the application of the mind.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, for the sake of the multitude of bodhisattvas in this assembly, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, we pray that you will expound the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice:
how they should contemplate, how they should maintain their resolve, and what they should do when sentient beings have not yet attained awakening."
"Through skillful means and right reflection, having heard the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, my mind became bewildered and distressed;
I was unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment. I pray that you will arouse compassion and provide an explanation through skillful means."
(Zongmi said: "It is called the Universal Eye because this dharma-gate causes one to contemplate that body and mind have no substantial essence;

that the faculties, consciousnesses, sense objects, and environments—whether mundane or supramundane, one's own body or another's body—are all pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm, universally equaling all Buddhas.
When contemplative practice is perfected and such a realm is suddenly perceived, this is the true Universal Eye. This contains compassion.)

"Wisdom" refers to the universal vision of the purity of all phenomena; this is the Universal Eye of Great Wisdom. To universally see all sentient beings attaining Buddhahood is the Universal Eye of Great Compassion.
(Pei Xiu said: "To cause them all to awaken universally—'opening and showing' refers to the capacity to transform, while 'awakening and entering' refers to those being transformed.
Regarding the present sutra, from this point forward, the Buddha's response makes full use of what was previously revealed by the Tathāgata.)"
Taking the pure *āśraya-parivṛtti* of the *bodhicitta* as the foundation, one contemplates the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—and extinguishes mental images.

Boundless space is manifested by that which is awakened; because this awakening is perfectly luminous, it reveals the purity of the mind, even to the point of being equal to all Buddhas. This is precisely what is meant by universally causing others to attain enlightenment.
Mount Shān said: "Regarding what is meant by 'Puyan requests the gradual stages of cultivation': Puxian’s inquiry was profound, and the Tathāgata answered in accordance with the principle.
First one seeks to eliminate the maladies of the mind, and only thereafter do the myriad practices together.
Yet some, hearing the previous teaching that 'knowing illusion is itself detachment, requiring no further expedient means and no gradual stages,' claim:"

Once this is known, there is nothing further to cultivate. However, the Universal Eye (Puyan), wishing to ensure that the teachings are complete and perfect, requests the opening of the gateway for the practice of cultivation.

The following sections are all presented as distinct categories: "Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which consists of investigating and discerning the true and the false.
"Abiding and Maintaining" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*): having realized the wondrous realm, one dwells securely within it and maintains it without loss.
...and universally cause them to attain awakening. This is similar to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which intends to cause sentient beings to "open, show, awaken, and enter.

Here, "opening" subsumes "showing," and "awakening" subsumes "entering. From the words "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) onwards, it conversely clarifies that upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, one should reflect through skillful means (*upāya*).
This is immediate enlightenment. To say "one who hears this samādhi" refers to the aforementioned Dharma-door of Detaching from Illusion. It is a provisional designation for skillful means.

As for the term "provisional designation," it is because the nature of awakening is fundamentally perfect and delusive phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; in reality, there is nothing to be cultivated.
However, because those who have first attained awakening find it difficult to suddenly bring an end to their deluded habits, one must request that within the state of non-cultivation,
the provisional means of cultivation be explained.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

It is well that you are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance, as well as the various provisional means of explanation.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake. Son of Good Family, if you wish to seek..."
The Tathāgata’s pure and perfect circle of awakening-mind should be contemplated with right mindfulness to remain far removed from all illusions.

First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one should firmly maintain the prohibitive precepts, settle the assembly, and sit in meditative seclusion within a quiet chamber, constantly forming this thought:
(Zongmi said: "Right mindfulness" is annotated as "non-mindfulness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Mindfulness is the work of Māra;
non-mindfulness is the Seal of the Dharma. The treatise further says: "One who is free from the marks of mindfulness is equal to the realm of empty space. It also says:

"All sentient beings are not called awakened because, from the very beginning, their thoughts have continued in succession, never departing from mindfulness. Therefore, we know that non-mindfulness is awakening.)
"This is right mindfulness. (Someone asked: "Practicing in a quiet room and dwelling among the assembly—how can these not be contradictory?

Zongmi said: "There are two explanations for this. First, because root-natures differ: some have much dullness and require the exhortation of the assembly to stimulate them; others have much restlessness [and thus require solitude].")

You should desist from external conditions. It is not for the sake of a single person that two practices are undertaken; rather, it is because one must train equally in both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This refers to the practice of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), which requires that cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) support one another.

You must rely on a virtuous friend who shares the same views, with whom you may discuss the gates of the Dharma all day long, ensuring that your application of the mind does not go astray. To err by even a hair’s breadth is to lose the way by a thousand miles. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says:
It is not necessarily sitting that constitutes "seated meditation" (yan-zuo).
As the Mountain said: "When the World-Honored One addressed Puyan, he first pointed directly at the essential point, saying: 'The pure, perfect, awakened mind.'"

Furthermore, he points to the previous analysis and explanation of being free from illusion as the foundation for initiating practice. This is because if one clings to phenomena as having fixed, substantial reality, then contemplative practice will not be accomplished;
therefore, it is necessary to take what preceded as a preliminary skillful means. "Right mindfulness" is non-mindfulness.
Right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and the departure from illusion (*māyā-vigama*) mutually establish one another. Because of the departure from illusion, there is right mindfulness;

because of right mindfulness, there is the departure from illusion. Why is this? If external phenomena exist, then internal conceptual thoughts arise; if internal conceptual thoughts exist, then external phenomena are perceived.

Pointing to both of these together at the beginning of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), *śamatha*—which is translated here as "stopping" (*zhi*)—is [the practice of] stopping. This stopping is...

Definition: The commentary below explains that "practice" refers to ultimate stillness (*parama-śānti*). Since there are varying degrees of depth in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the term "Tathāgata" is specified to distinguish this from coarse, shallow, heterodox, or Hinayana concentrations.
If one observes the precepts with a distracted mind, one is incapable of entering this gate of contemplation;

therefore, concentration is established first, followed by the precepts. One who firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts is single-mindedly detached from sensory objects and resolutely intends not to transgress them; this is called...
To persistently guard the sense-faculties and restrain body and speech is called "prohibitive precepts" (*śīla*).
As for "settling the assembly," these are those who share the same practice and the same view; since their conduct is identical, they refine one another and consult together.
Because it serves as a condition for the long path, one must dwell in a place of peace. "Sitting in quietude" (*yàn-zuò*) means to remain silent.

Sitting is for the purpose of restraining the body; when the body is settled, the mind is at peace; when the mind is at leisure, the environment is tranquil. Desiring to settle both body and mind, one must have a quiet room.
To "constantly maintain this mindfulness" means to always observe in this manner at all times—whether standing, sitting, walking, or lying down.

This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements: that is to say, the hair of the head and body, the nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impure physical matter all return to earth;
saliva, nasal mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of feces and urine all return to water;
warmth returns to fire; and movement returns to wind. Now, as these four great elements separate from one another—here now...
Where, then, does this delusory body reside?
(It is a false conjunction of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:
"When this body is born, it shares the same nature as the four great elements of its parents; it is a kalala-body. If there were only the earth element and no water element, for example—"
It is like a person grasping dry flour or ashes; they can never be made into a cohesive mass.
If there were only the water element and no earth element, it would be like oil or water, which lack solidity and would immediately flow away and disperse.

If there were only the earth and water elements and no fire element, it would be like a lump of flesh in the shade during the summer months, which would quickly rot and decay without the light of the sun. If there were only the earth, water, and fire elements...
Regarding the realm of no-wind, there is no growth. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also states: "Because the four great elements combine, they are conventionally designated as a body.
As it says: "The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind. Because the four great elements combine, they are conventionally designated as a body.
The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. Thus, this scriptural passage further divides the four great elements, each returning to its respective source.

That hair, fur, nails, teeth, and so forth return to earth is because solidity and firmness constitute the quality of earth. That saliva and mucus return to water is because moisture constitutes water.

That warmth returns to fire—since this "warmth" (*uṣman*) is the fundamental basis of the four great elements and not merely wind—it is therefore also referred to as "warmth" within the elements of water and fire.
That movement and transformation return to wind is [as stated in] the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
It is said: This body is without agency; it is driven by the power of the winds. When one observes correctly, each of the four great elements returns to its own source, which is termed "separation.
Furthermore, while virtue possesses form and obstruction and is thus heavy and stagnant, the wind has no form or obstruction and is light and buoyant.
When entities are fundamentally opposed, even water and fire contend with and supplant one another; thus we know that the four great elements are mutually contradictory and each distinct.
I do not yet know to which of these elements my body belongs. If it belonged to them collectively, it would constitute four selves.
If it belonged to none of them collectively, then there should be a body-self existing apart from the four. Therefore, it is said: "Where, then, does this delusory body reside?"
One then knows that this body is ultimately without substance; it exists as a manifestation of conjunction and is truly like an illusion.

Through the provisional combination of the four conditions, the six sense organs falsely arise. These six organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally to form a false accumulation of conditioning energy within.
That which appears to have the characteristics of an object is conventionally designated as "mind.
(Pei Xiu’s Discourse states: Mind has no intrinsic nature; it arises only by relying upon objects. The nature of objects is fundamentally empty, yet they manifest due to the mind.)
When the sense faculties and their objects combine, it appears as if there is a mind that perceives them. Yet, when one investigates both internally and externally, what is its actual substance?

One wanders through the cycle of birth and death because of a failure to understand this mind; were one able to understand it, Perfect Enlightenment would manifest of itself. Thus, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "The nature of madness subsides of its own accord."
"Cessation is itself bodhi; it is supremely pure, wondrous, and luminous, not obtained from others. Zongmi said:
"By means of the preceding investigation and contemplation, one perceives the principle of reality as it is. One definitively knows that the four great elements are not the self;
they are merely designated as a 'body' based on their conjunction, yet they possess no substantial entity. The conjunction of the four great elements constitutes a single form."
Above this form, there are the six sense organs. The four great elements constitute the interior, while the six sense organs constitute the exterior.

Through the union of the internal and external, this body is provisionally formed. From these internal organs and external objects, deluded consciousness is induced, and its discursive contemplation continues without ceasing.
Moment by moment it arises and ceases; not even for an instant does it remain still. When conditions combine, it exists; when conditions disperse, it is non-existent.

Upon investigating its own essence, it is found to be utterly unobtainable. Therefore, it is said that "mind" is a provisional designation. Although this deluded mind arises dependently through provisional conditions, [it lacks any inherent reality].

It does not depart from the constituent energy of the true mind; hence it is called "conditioned energy" (*yuanqi*). To say it is "resembling" [something] clarifies that it is not substantially existent.
"Conditioned marks" (*yuanxiang*) refers to the marks of conceptual deliberation.
Good son, this deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense objects. When the four great elements are analyzed and disintegrated, no sense objects can be found.
Within them, the conditions for sense objects each return to their dissolution; ultimately, there is no perceiving mind to be seen.

(Question: The last three lines following "no dust can be apprehended" also speak of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā*). How can they be categorically judged to belong solely to the emptiness of persons (*pudgalasūnyatā*)?
Answer: This refers to the dispersal of the objects of perception; it primarily reveals the emptiness of the mind. Therefore, the conclusion states: "no mind can be perceived.")
Both body and mind belong entirely to the grasping at a self (this is the first emptiness of phenomena).

As it is said: "The mind relies upon the six sense objects; the sense objects depend upon the four great elements. Since the four great elements have no intrinsic substance, the six sense objects are empty."

Therefore, it is said that they "dissipate and perish. Once the objects of perception have perished, the substance of the mind is immediately empty; thus, it is definitively judged that they "ultimately do not exist.
As for the term "perceptual mind," it refers to the mind of the preceding perceptual breath.
"Good son, because the illusory body of those sentient beings ceases, the illusory mind also ceases. Because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease.
Because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion itself also ceases. When the cessation of illusion ceases, that which is not illusory does not cease.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the brightness appears."

When illusion is extinguished and that extinction itself ceases, then the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is seen—like the moon emerging when clouds disperse, or like a mirror becoming clear when dust is removed.
This does not mean that the absence of clouds is itself called the moon; rather, it is simply that the moon is seen in the place where there are no clouds.
Likewise, this does not mean that the absence of illusion is itself *tathatā*; rather, it is simply that the true principle is seen in the place where there is no illusion.

Mount Shān said: Previously, one sought the non-existence of a self within the body and mind; therefore, it is called the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Now, the body, mind, and their objects are each empty in themselves;
therefore, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). However, the body and so forth are fundamentally empty; they do not become empty for the first time now through cessation.
Thus, a sutra says: "Form is itself emptiness; it is not that form ceases to be empty. It is only because of delusion that one clings to existence.
Now, the adherence to the notion that "the beginning is non-existent" refers to the meaning of cessation. Because illusory objects cease, the cessation of the illusion itself also ceases.

This means that when there is the emotion of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), one perceives the arising of the illusion; when there is the wisdom of observation, one perceives the cessation of the illusion.

Because it is contrasted with the arising of the illusion, one speaks of the "cessation of the illusion"; because it is contrasted with emotional attachment, one speaks of "wisdom. All such phenomena of mutual opposition are...
They belong to dependent origination; that which is dependently originated is signless, and therefore all are said to be "extinguished. The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* says:
"There is no eye-faculty, and so forth, up to no wisdom and no attainment. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness;
since wisdom cannot apprehend existence or non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion. The phrase "that which is not illusion does not extinguish" precisely clarifies this.

...it reveals that the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is fundamentally pure and perfectly luminous, a single essence that is entirely true and not attained through cultivation.
Although all illusions may cease, the self-nature remains eternally present; as it does not arise dependent on conditions, it is called "non-illusion.

The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "If one attains the empty mind, the mind is no longer illusory. However, in contrast to the preceding state where delusions are exhausted, this is explained as *tathatā* (suchness). If...
