According to our own school, it is simply named Perfect Enlightenment. The subsequent metaphor is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, the brightness appears.

Although one speaks of "polishing the mirror," it is actually polishing away the dust. What is called the cultivation of the Way is merely the removal of delusions; for the nature of the mirror is inherently bright.

It is not obtained from without. When obscured by defilements, it is hidden; when polished, it is revealed. Although its states of being hidden and revealed differ, the luminous nature remains unchanged.

Now, it is said that clinging to persons and phenomena is the defilement; investigating and contemplating according to reality is the polishing; the true mind’s original enlightenment is the luminosity;
and the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena is the manifestation.
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are entirely illusory defilements. When the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions become pure.
(As Shan said: 'The faculties, objects, and all dharmas, as well as the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, are universally pure.

This is because, due to the defilements and obscurations of body and mind, one falsely clings to self and other, thereby creating limitations and obstructions. Since the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, it is said thus.)"
As the Mountain says: "Illusion" (māyā) means that which is empty and illusory, having no substantial reality. "Defilement" (mala) is a term for dust and grime;
because one is deluded by illusory appearances, one grasps and becomes attached to them, thereby defiling the pure mind. Thus it is called "illusory defilement.

Although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess bodies and minds, because they realize these are like illusions and do not grasp at signs, they lack the sense of being defiled; therefore, [the Buddhas] are not [illusory defilements].

Defilements. Because one realizes that they are empty like an illusion, they are not illusions. When the self is empty and phenomena are quiescent, what is there that is not penetrated? Therefore, it is said that the ten directions are pure.
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel which reflects the five colors, appearing as each respective color according to its direction. All...
The ignorant person sees that mani-jewel as truly possessing five colors.
(Zongmi says: This is because the metaphors employed for the jewel and the mirror differ; therefore, he marks this point again to inform us.

However, the previous metaphor of the mirror was merely one-sidedly bright, and it further stated that [the colors] appear through polishing, which represents the principle of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*)—only after shattering attachments does [the truth manifest].)
"Manifestation" (xian) is a name derived from its contrast with attachment. Now, this mani-jewel is fundamentally pure and fundamentally luminous, illuminating the ten directions simultaneously;
this serves to manifest the principle of the ultimate Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Mount Shān said: "The essence of the maṇi jewel is translucent and pure, free from all blemish, and devoid of any color-form.
Because its nature is pure, all color-forms appear within it when they encounter it. The five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—each manifest according to their respective directions.
A fool, failing to understand the substance of the jewel, sees only the blue, yellow, and other colors, and thus does not see the jewel itself."

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Ordinary beings perceive all phenomena merely as they revolve according to their various marks; failing to understand that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they do not see the Buddha.
If these are assigned to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the mani jewel is a metaphor for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is precisely the principle revealed previously. The manifestation of forms is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the aforementioned illusion.
The fixed perception of blue or yellow by a fool is a metaphor for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the aforementioned dust and grime.
"Good son, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding appropriately to each according to its kind.
Those who are deluded likewise claim that the pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such inherent characteristics of body and mind."
(As Mount Shān said: "Responding to each according to its kind" refers to the various preceding illusory transformations arising from the awakened mind.
The passage beginning with "Those who are ignorant" clarifies that although Perfect Enlightenment manifests, it is not its fixed reality; this is likewise so, corresponding to the previous metaphor.)
Because of this, they cannot remain far removed from illusion and transformation. Therefore, I say that body and mind are illusory defilements.

In contrast to those who have left behind illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva. When defilements are exhausted and their opposites eliminated, there is neither the defilement nor the one who speaks of it.
Good son, because these Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age have realized all illusions and extinguished their reflected images, at that time they immediately attain the Unconditioned.

Only then is it pure. Boundless space is that which is manifested by awakening (the character "zhě" [者] actually applies to both phrases; that is, the Bodhisattva who faces defilement, and the one who is called a Buddha). As Shan said:
"That which is manifested by awakening is what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* when it says: 'If there is a person who gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, [then the ten...]"
[They will] vanish all at once like space.
Zongmi said: "The above first explains the reason for these manifestations (*traces*). Yet these manifestations arise one after another."
They also follow one another in being brushed away. Originally, because sentient beings falsely cling to illusory transformations, the Buddha spoke of them as "illusory defilements" (*māyā-mala*).
Because sentient beings rely on the teaching to become free from these defilements, they are further called "Bodhisattvas.

When the defilements are exhausted and their opposites eliminated, it is said that the illusory defilements are like colors within a gem; realizing they are fundamentally non-existent is what is meant by "exhaustion. Since the defilements to be abandoned have been completely exhausted:

If there is no wisdom regarding detachment, how can there be the establishment [of such a state]? Since there is no wisdom that acts as an antidote, how can there be a person who gives rise to wisdom?
Since the grasping at depth and shallowness is fundamentally non-existent, how can there be one who expounds the teachings? Therefore, both are non-existent. "Good son," and so forth.
The "proclamation" and the "pointing to the root" refer to that which is realized; it is the accomplishment of the practice of contemplation through the realization of all illusions.
Because reflected images are extinguished, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) also vanishes. One attains directionless purity, meaning that the illusory body takes precedence.

When looking externally at east or west, since the mark of self (*ātman*) no longer exists, what further direction or location could there be? Nevertheless, space is separate from consciousness and is not real either.
Because [the nature] exists, it is shrouded by delusion and awakening; when one perceives emptiness at the locus of awakening, the shadows of sensory objects dissolve.

Emptiness is fundamentally awakening itself. "Manifestation" refers to the appearance of awakening as emptiness dissolves; "arising" refers to the opening of the mind when delusion is exhausted. Examining these from every perspective, both are without boundaries.
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure. Because the mind is pure, the objects of sight are pure.

Because the objects of sight are pure, the faculty of the eye is pure. Because the faculty of the eye is pure, the visual consciousness is pure. Because the visual consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure.
Because hearing is pure, the faculty of the ear is pure. Because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure.
Because consciousness is pure, the perception of objects is pure. This applies likewise to the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
(Consciousness possesses five meanings. It is designated according to its faculty. First, it is consciousness that depends upon the faculty, not because of the objective form.

This is because it is said to arise determinately [from the faculty], as in the case of the blind who do not see, and so forth. Second, it is consciousness produced by the faculty; when the faculty undergoes transformation, the consciousness necessarily undergoes transformation.
For example, if the eye-faculty perceives blue as yellow, it is not the case that the consciousness is destroyed when the object is destroyed. Third, it is consciousness that belongs to the faculty.)
Because consciousness arises by following the sense faculties through its seeds, it is not the case that the seeds of form follow the seeds of consciousness.

Fourth, the consciousness that assists the sense faculties is such that, through the conjunction of the faculty and consciousness, what is experienced by consciousness causes benefit or harm to the faculty; this does not apply to the objective field.

Fifth, just like the sense faculties, both the faculty and consciousness are comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*); it is not necessarily the case that the same applies to those material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

Regarding sentient beings: because the five faculties are preeminent in terms of ultimate reality, they are said to be the bases [of consciousness]. If one relies on their arising from mind, all are termed mental consciousness (manovijñāna), for all six arise based upon the mind.
As the Mountain said: "Because the *Awakened Enlightenment* (*Vimalakīrti*) is luminous. This traces back to the previously revealed cause of purity.

Because [delusions] are brushed away and obliterated, one attains perfect luminosity, revealing the purity of the mind. This means that whereas the deluded mind clings to phenomena within the mind, now one perceives the *dharmatā*;
since all phenomena are empty, it is called "pure. Because the mind is pure, one perceives the purity of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). That is to say:
Because of my mind’s conceptual grasping, I perceive all forms and appearances. Due to this grasping at appearances, I see that these very perceptions are themselves the objects (*viṣaya*).
When the "pure phrase" speaks of "seeing," it merely cites the word "seeing" without explicitly mentioning "objects"; this is sufficient to clearly demonstrate that seeing itself is the object.

It is not an external object. The same applies to hearing and the other senses. Regarding the phrase "the purity of the eye-faculty," the remaining five [faculties] are to be understood by this same principle.
All six are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are the supports for consciousness and because they are capable of producing consciousness.

The first five are named according to how they arise from their own seeds as their own manifest activity, with pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) produced by the four great elements serving as their basis. The mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is the seventh consciousness.

Because it grasps outwardly by giving rise to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the phrase "the faculties are purified" and below applies this same principle to the remaining five [consciousnesses].

All are called "consciousness" because they differ in kind according to the objects of the six faculties. When ordinary beings grasp and cling more deeply, reckoning things as "self" and "mine," and through various false attachments, they grasp at objects according to their circumstances and discriminate the six sense-fields; this is called the mental consciousness. It is also named...

The consciousness of separation. Furthermore, it is said that this is called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*). From the phrase "the purity of consciousness" onwards, all should be understood in this manner.
Good son, because the sense faculties are pure, the objects of form are pure; because form is pure, the objects of sound are pure; [and] fragrance...
Taste, touch, and mental objects are likewise.

As Mount Shān said: "When one speaks of form and so forth, it is because they are what is apprehended by the eye and the other [senses]. Form possesses both general and specific characteristics; here, we are referring specifically to the latter."
"Only the single object of the dharma-dust (*dharmālambana*) apprehended by the mind is common to all.
Zongmi said: "The reason all six are called 'dusts' (*rajas*) is that they defile the mental consciousness; this is spoken with reference to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
They are also called the 'six objects' (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); this is a term applicable to both ordinary beings and sages (*ārya*)."
"Good son, because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure;
and the fire and wind elements are likewise so."

Pei Xiu said: "This means that within the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), one does not take up the meaning of the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*) which draws forth the mind; rather, one takes up directly the substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

As the Mountain [Master] said: "The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states that each of the four great elements has two aspects, namely the internal and the external. Regarding the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), there are these two."

The internal refers to all that is solid within one's own body and the bodies of others, such as hair, body hair, and so forth. The external refers to all that is solid outside the body, such as earth, wood, and so forth.
Regarding the two aspects of the water element: internally, it is the hot substance and the characteristic of heat within the body that can digest food and drink;

externally, it is the hot substance and the characteristic of heat outside the body that can bring about ripening and so forth. Regarding the two aspects of the wind element: internally... [the text continues].
The nature of wind: wind is named "swift. It abides in the four limbs and so forth, as well as in external bodies and the like.
Good son, because the nature of all real marks is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, [all are pure].
The many bodies are pure. Because the many bodies are pure, in this way it extends even to the universal awakening and purity of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
(The *Anantārthasūtra* says: "Thus, non-characteristic is not non-characteristic; non-non-characteristic is characteristic. This is called the true characteristic.")
The purity of many bodies means that all sentient beings do not grasp at appearances, for they are identical with the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-āśraya*).
Master Zongmi said: "Master Zhigong stated: 'Because my body is empty, all phenomena are empty; the thousands of kinds and myriad species are entirely the same. Zongmi [comments]:

The perfect enlightenment and purity of sentient beings in the ten directions—this is precisely when one person awakens to their own nature and realizes that it is the fundamental nature of all sentient beings."
Purity does not mean that many people practicing the Way will all become Buddhas. As it is said:
"All phenomena that possess marks are entirely false and illusory, for they arise from conditions; by comprehending these conditions, one enters into reality."
This is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Only this true mark has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning;

it cannot be defiled by any delusive phenomena (*mṛṣādharma*). Although it appears as if defiled due to delusion, now that its original purity is realized, it is termed "purity of nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).

Because its nature is pure, the single body is pure. Through the aforementioned realization, one attains the roots, consciousnesses, objects, and the great [elements], as well as all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

All phenomena ultimately return to the purity of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Only then is perfection achieved. Having personally realized the principle of the true mark, one also perceives that all sentient beings share this same pure true mark.

Regarding the passage below concerning "the purity of many bodies," it means that by means of the correct wisdom of *prajñā*, one universally contemplates sentient beings, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the nature of untainted wisdom as being fundamentally [pure].
It is complete.
Good son, because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive, the nature of the sense organs and the nature of the sense objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled.

Because the sense organs and sense objects are not destroyed [as distinct entities], even up to the gates of *dhāraṇī*, they are neither destroyed nor intermingled, like hundreds of thousands of lamps.
The light illuminates the entire room; that light is pervasive, neither destroyed nor mixed.
(Zongmi says: *Dhāraṇī* refers to a Bodhisattva who has attained total retention (*saṃdhāraṇa*), for within each and every phenomenon they maintain all phenomena.
The metaphor of the hundred thousand lamps means that once the light of a single lamp has filled a room, another lamp is added.)
The light is also perfectly full. Each of the hundreds of thousands of lamp-lights is likewise so; they do not obstruct one another, nor are they confused or intermingled.

As it says in the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra*: "Because that wondrous enlightened nature is all-pervasive. This refers to the nature of the basis, which serves as the reason why each individual phenomenon is all-pervasive and unobstructed.
The nature of the sense organs (*indriya*) and the nature of the objects (*viṣaya*)—these each refer to the self-nature of the sense organs and the objects themselves.
"Nature" does not mean that the faculties are extinguished and the objects are subsumed, returning to a single nature. It means there is neither destruction nor confusion;

that is, both the faculties and the objects are phenomenal dharmas (*dharma*). From "the faculties and objects are not destroyed" onwards, following the pattern of the preceding seven sections, it is the same for every phenomenon.

Therefore, it says "up to and including" (乃至) and so forth. As in the passage "like a hundred thousand lamps," the empty space within the room is used as a metaphor for the *dharmadhātu*, while the luminous characteristics of the lamps are used as metaphors for the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). This means that the light of a single lamp can accommodate many luminous characteristics.
That is, a single light-form pervades many light-forms; each and every one is likewise so, layer upon layer without end.

The phenomena and dharmas of the preceding seven sections should all be understood by this analogy; thus can their mutual containment and universal pervasion be seen. This is what is meant. Why is this so?
Because they are manifested solely by the true mind, and are all like illusions, dreams, or reflections; therefore, they are not [separate from] the nature upon which they depend.
Because they are neither identical nor different, one can enter the many within the one; thus, the one encompasses the many and so forth.
Good son, because awakening is perfected, you should know that a Bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas;

they do not loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nor do they crave *nirvāṇa*; they do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor do they despise those who violate them; they do not prize long-standing practice, nor...
Do not disparage beginners. Why? Because they possess all-encompassing awakening.
(The *Śāstra* states: "The meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of mind being free from discursive thought.

Here, it means being free from the eight mental states previously mentioned—namely, seeking, aversion, love, respect, hatred, heaviness, lightness, and so forth. These eight objects are cited to reveal the nature of the mind.)
As Mount says: "Because of the accomplishment of awakening" refers collectively to the passage beginning with "perfectly manifesting the dharma-realm.
By means of this, one attains a realm identical to that of the Buddha. As for what is meant by "identical": regarding the four pairs of dharmas, there is no mind of superior power;

because it is like the Buddha's state regarding the three objects of mindfulness, it is said to be "identical. Regarding the reason for this identity, the sutra itself provides the inquiry and explanation:
Because of universal awakening, it is like the light of the eyes that clearly perceives objects before one; this light is perfect and complete, free from both aversion and attachment. Why is this?
Because the essence of light is non-dual and devoid of aversion and attachment.
(Shouleng says: "The eyes look about, but it is just like [seeing] within a mirror, without any further analysis. Your consciousness [is within that]"). Zongmi says:
"Light is the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Since it is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no aversion or attachment."
Good son, when these bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age cultivate this mind and attain its fulfillment, there is neither cultivation nor fulfillment therein.

Perfect enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent extinction, non-dual. Within it, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* eons, as numerous as the sands of unspeakably many Ganges Rivers.

As Mount Shān said: "The *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* concludes by stating that Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is illumination within stillness, while Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabodhi*) is stillness within illumination.
To say now that one is 'identical to the Buddha' carries the meaning of Equal Enlightenment; therefore, it is said that there is universal illumination within quiescent extinction.

Both the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* state that in the fruit of Buddhahood, there are no distinct qualities of form or sound; only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain. This pertains to the three worlds.
Because they are fused and unimpeded: the world is the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*); sentient beings are the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*);
and attaining Buddhahood is the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment (*jñānasambuddhaloka*).
Mount Shān said: "To speak of 'no cultivation' and 'no accomplishment' is to obliterate the traces of the preceding mind.

If these are not obliterated, then even if one is free from hatred or respect, one still perceives holding and disparaging, and so forth. Therefore, it is necessary to obliterate them before one’s vision can accord with that of the Buddha.
From this point forward, the text correctly demonstrates this accord: 'Perfect Enlightenment shines universally; it is quiescent and non-dual. This arises because the self is empty; it is merely..."

This is awakening-illumination. How could there be the duality of distinctions between ordinary beings and sages? It is the merging into the non-mind of the single suchness; for it is the eternal stillness of all phenomena.
Thus, universal illumination is its function, and quiescent extinction is its essence. This is the ultimate limit of the Buddha—reaching the pinnacle of quiescence and illumination.
"Within this" means within the midst of quiescence and illumination. *Asaṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇) here translates as "innumerable. This is...
This is the foremost among the ten great numbers in the *Avataṃsaka* and is frequently employed in the sūtras and śāstras; therefore, it is cited here. The ten are:

asaṃkhyeya (incalculable), apramāṇa (immeasurable), ananta (boundless), asama (unequaled), agaṇeya (uncountable), atulya (incomparable), acintya (inconceivable), amita (unmeasurable), anabhilāpya (ineffable), and anabhilāpyānabhilāpya (ineffably ineffable). As for "the sands of the Ganges," this refers to the sands within the River Gaṅgā.
It is all sand. This river flows out from the eastern side of Lake Anavatapta. When it first emerges from the elephant's mouth, it is forty *li* in circumference;
golden sand flows mixed with the water. The sand is as fine as flour, and because it is so fine, its quantity is vast.
The worlds of all Buddhas are like flowers in the sky: arising and appearing in confusion, neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor liberated.
Only then does one realize that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the beginning; birth and death, as well as nirvana, are like a dream from yesterday.
(As Mount said: "Chaos arises and chaos ceases. This has three meanings. First, all worlds without exception depend upon deluded thought;

since thought does not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), the worlds also arise and cease without ceasing. Second, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Because defiled sentient beings dwell [there], the world becomes defiled;
because sentient beings of great merit dwell [there], it becomes defiled-and-pure. Faith and understanding...)
Because Bodhisattvas dwell therein, they bring about both purity and defilement; this is the third point, the characteristic of formation and destruction. As it is said:
"The worlds of all Buddhas are calculated by means of the higher *asaṃkhyeya* numbers; such is the numerical count of these worlds.
Nevertheless, all lands—whether pure or defiled—are governed by the Buddha, and are therefore called 'Buddha-worlds. They are like flowers in the sky, meaning that their conditions are non-existent."
As for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the entire body is itself the Truth. One sees that all worlds abide like illusions, arising in disorder and ceasing in disorder.
It is said that worlds are infinite and innumerable; when viewed as a whole, their arising and ceasing are profuse and variegated—neither identical with nor separate from [the nature].

This clarifies that these worlds are neither identical with Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) nor separate from Perfect Enlightenment. There is neither bondage nor liberation. (The text continues.)
Regarding "above and below": "Above" refers to the fact that the world has neither purity nor defilement; "below" refers to the fact that sentient beings have fundamentally attained Buddhahood.

"Initial realization" (*shijue*) means that one can only know [this truth] once the practice of contemplation is perfected. "Fundamental attainment" (*bencheng*) refers to original enlightenment (*benjue*);
whether one knows it or not, one is fundamentally a Buddha. Thus, birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; this is called the absence of initial enlightenment.
...the difference between them. Because the four marks are fundamentally one with awakening, O son of good family, they are like a dream from yesterday;
you should know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going.
That which is realized is without gain and without loss, without grasping and without abandoning. As for that which realizes it, there is no...
It is non-ceasing, without reliance, and without extinction. Within this realization, there is no subject and no object;
ultimately, there is neither realization nor one who realizes. The nature of all phenomena is equal and indestructible.
Good son, those bodhisattvas practice in this way, progress through these stages, contemplate in this way, maintain themselves in this way, and employ skillful means in this way.
To attain enlightenment and seek such a Dharma is not to be confused or distressed.
(Zongmi said: To see birth-and-death and nirvana as a dream is to call it the true nature of Perfect Enlightenment, identical to the realm of the Buddhas.)
There are two intended meanings here. First, wherever there is a dream as the dependent, there must necessarily be a person as its basis;

for the dream is the spirit’s excursion of that person, being merely a manifestation of their sensory faculties and lacking any separate substance. Second, one simply realizes that the essence of the dream is empty and non-existent.

One immediately realizes the reality of one's own self. For those who are deluded regarding their own selves, because they cling to dreams, there must be the clarity of great awakening within the realm of the great dream.

“As like a mountain” means “like a dream from yesterday”; this summarizes the preceding statement. “One should know” and below refers to the fact that during delusion, birth-and-death does not arise and nirvana does not cease;
yet upon awakening, it is not that birth-and-death is extinguished and nirvana is produced.

When one contemplates in accordance with the essence, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing, and no coming or going. Regarding the realm realized, one naturally attains the true and abandons the false. Abandon—
Grasping the coarse as sublime, the mind that is capable of realization is entirely without discrimination; it is free from the four maladies.
Within this realization, subject and object are extinguished, and there is no one who realizes. Those who seek the Buddha-way should practice in this manner.
Therefore, the subsequent passage concludes by restating the words of the question.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, if all sentient beings have been enlightened from the very beginning, for what reason do they still possess all manner of ignorance?
If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the start, by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further declare that they have been enlightened from the beginning? Ten.
Ordinary beings first attain the Buddha-way and subsequently give rise to ignorance; when will all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to any afflictions?

We pray that you will open the secret treasury for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age, so that they may hear such a sūtra teaching of the definitive meaning (nītārtha) and forever sever doubt and regret.
[Supplementary Note: "Vajra" is named after its metaphorical qualities. A vajra is both firm and sharp; when held upright, nothing can destroy it, and being sharp, it can destroy all things.
The wisdom of this Bodhisattva is likewise: afflictions cannot invade it, and external māras cannot shake it—this is its firmness.
It can shatter all obstacles and sever the doubts of sentient beings—this is its sharpness. Therefore, three levels of profundity arise.
The profundity [of this teaching] is difficult to fathom; it is intended to dispel the doubts of the degenerate age. Once doubt is eliminated, one immediately possesses inexhaustible merit;
therefore, it is further called a "Treasury" (*pitaka*). As Mount Shan said: "In general discussion, 'doubt' has the nature of indecision and can obstruct the mind of faith.

'Regret' is a state of instability. For those entering the Path, if they have not yet reached a definitive resolution regarding whether sentient beings and Buddhas are identical or different, they may sometimes..."
Having practiced for a long time with much effort, he again felt doubt and regret;
therefore, he requested that [the Buddha] definitively sever [his doubts]. As the Mountain said: "Regarding this question of Vajra, there are three difficulties. His first doubt is:

'If one has been a Buddha from the very beginning, why is there still the existence of all ignorance? This doubt implies that the Truth could actually give rise to delusion. From the phrase 'If there were various ignorances' onwards, the doubt is as follows:"

This refers to claiming that what is false is true. The section beginning with "Sentient beings of the ten directions differ" takes up this point and grants it for the sake of argument, only to charge it with the fault of infinite regress.
The intent behind these three objections above is as follows: If one is fundamentally a Buddha, how could afflictions arise?

If they were to falsely arise within that state of non-arising, then when a Tathāgata attains Buddhahood—remaining within that same fundamental state of non-arising—he too would necessarily have to falsely arise [into affliction]. Thus, he would become...

Regarding the meaning of "Buddha" and so forth: whether [sentient beings] are born [as Buddhas] or not should be uniform. If they were uniformly born, then the result—the Buddha—would be equal [to all]; if they were not uniform, then the cause would contradict manifest reality.
Since it is untenable from either perspective, it is for this reason that it is said thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:

"Good son, the beginning and end, birth and death, prior and subsequent, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, arising and ceasing of all worlds—these continuous successions of thought-moments, their cycles of recurrence, and their various acts of grasping and rejecting, are all saṃsāra.
To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment while still remaining within saṃsāra is for one's nature to be identical with the cycle of transmigration. If..."
To be exempt from saṃsāra—such a thing is impossible.
(From this point downward, the text analyzes saṃsāra; that is to say, it refers to the mind that dwells only in the conditioned and is thus directed toward saṃsāra.)
[Supplementary Note states: "Beginning" refers to the initial transformation; "end" refers to ultimate realization. "Arising" means that the new constantly emerges;

"extinction" means that every thought-moment falls away. "Before" refers to the past; "after" refers to the future. "Existence" refers to the kalpa of becoming; "non-existence" refers to the empty kalpa.
[The mind] is the kalpa of formation; it is the kalpa of dissolution; it is the arising of active manifestation; [the mind] is subjugation. (Zongmi said:)

There are various forms of acceptance and rejection: regarding the faculties and the body, one regards suffering, coarseness, and obstruction as that which is to be rejected, and tranquility, subtlety, and detachment as that which is to be accepted;
regarding the vessel-world, one regards this Sahā world as that which is to be rejected, and that Land of Ultimate Bliss as that which is to be accepted.

Mount Shāna said: "This 'entirety of worlds' refers collectively to both the sentient and insentient realms. Both the realm of sentient beings and the realm of the vessel-world depend upon deluded thought;
because their basis—the continuity of arising and ceasing—is never severed, that which depends upon it likewise persists.

They revolve in cycles: the vessel-world, having been emptied, is formed again; the realm of sentient beings, having ceased, is born again. Thus, afflictions and karma continue to accumulate through habitual conditioning."
Karmic retribution is woven through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and cannot be obstructed or severed. "Grasping" (upādāna) refers to attachment and clinging to what is "mine";

"relinquishing" (prahāṇa) refers to wearying detachment from that which serves as the basis for suffering. Whether grasping or relinquishing, these various differences are all manifestations of the deluded, inverted mind—the very signs of saṃsāra.
As long as one has not emerged from saṃsāra, this is what is called "being able to contemplate."
Because the mind of saṃsāra is thus, the Perfect Enlightenment that is observed is likewise so. It is like seeing a real object in a dream; for the object, too, is a dream.
It is like the movement of the eyes, which can cause the still water to tremble; or like the fixed eye, by which a fire-brand is whirled; or like the clouds racing past the moon.
As for movement: when a boat travels, the shore appears to move; it is just like this.
(The eyes and the boat on the clouds are metaphors for the defiled mind of birth and death; the water, fire, moon, and shore are metaphors for Perfect Enlightenment.)
As Shan said: "The eyes move in succession, like the ripples on still water. Visual consciousness is sluggish, like a whirling firebrand forming the appearance of a wheel.
When clouds race, the moon seems to move; when a boat travels, the shore appears to shift—these can be seen through reflection."
Good son, while the various rotations have not yet ceased, even that object which supposedly abides beforehand cannot be found;

how much less so for one who revolves in birth and death, whose defiled mind has never been purified, and who contemplates the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment without returning to stillness? For this reason, you have given rise to the three delusions.
(The various revolutions have not yet ceased; the eyes are like a cloud-boat. That object previously abiding cannot be found; it is like water, fire, the moon, and the shore). As the Mountain says:
"The three delusions" refers to the aforementioned three kinds of doubt. Based on this indication in the concluding text, one may know [this].

This must first be considered a refutation of the root of doubt; it is not yet an answer. If it were a comprehensive response to one of the three difficulties within the triad, it would be inappropriate to summarize all three delusions at once. Let the wise examine this closely.
Good son, it is like the illusion of cataracts, which causes one to falsely perceive flowers in the sky.

If the illusion of the cataracts is removed, one cannot say that these cataracts have been extinguished and that they will ever arise again at some time. Why is this? Because the two phenomena—the cataract and the flower—do not exist in mutual dependence.
It is also like when flowers in the sky vanish into the void; one cannot say that empty space will ever give rise to them again.
It is like flowers in the sky. Why? Because emptiness fundamentally has no flowers; they neither arise nor cease. Birth-and-death and nirvana are both like arising and ceasing;
the perfect illumination of wondrous enlightenment is free from such floral obscurations.
[Question: Regarding those whose cataracts have been cured, it may happen that they reappear at another time; it is not necessarily certain that they will never recur.
How can this serve as a metaphor? [Answer: As for a metaphor, it merely takes up the events of a single occasion on that day and does not speak of one’s entire life.
It is simply like a fool who, having seen flowers in the morning, has his vision corrected by mealtime, yet perceives the flowers arising and ceasing in confusion, and thus calls them "cataracts."
They also arise and cease with equal speed; one must observe them moment by moment. Therefore it is said that [it is] "not so. (The commentary on the *Ming* states:

Ignorance and emptiness are not merely temporary existences or non-existences. What relation does the nature of awakening have to delusion or enlightenment? Since sentient beings are like flowers arising in the sky, in relation to whom could one further question ignorance?
Since ignorance and birth-and-death are empty, why blame the original attainment of Buddhahood? Empty flowers ultimately do not...)

He rose again. How could one who has attained the fruit-stage fall back into delusion? Because he has crossed over himself without ceasing, he perceives that the nature of awakening in others is still subject to transmigration.
If one understands it in this way, the three doubts are instantly dispelled.
Mount Shān said: It is like not knowing that the flowers exist because of the cataract, yet falsely clinging to them as arising from empty space.
Not realizing that one has lost touch with the truth, one gives rise to false horizontal cataracts; thus, the Truth is able to give rise to the delusion.

Once the cataract has been cured and the flowers are no longer seen, if one hears it said that they arose from the cataract, one will again cling to the thought, "When will I have another cataract? This serves as a metaphor for the delusions and perversions we have encountered until now, which lead to false perceptions.
Regarding saṃsāra: by hearing this Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, one realizes that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are pure.

One hears that delusion is eliminated through the cause [of awakening], and thus attains purity. This is not a wondrous gate newly acquired; yet, to cling to whether it is early or late is further delusion—just like asking when the cataract will ever clear.
Why is this? As stated below: the cataract does not wait for the flower, nor does the flower arise following the cataract.

It is merely due to the cataract that there is false seeing; the flowers do not actually arise. These two dharmas are each unaware of the other, let alone one being empty and the other being existent;
thus it is said they do not depend upon one another. Even if the mind is deluded, birth and death are nonetheless quiescent; it is simply because of delusion that [they appear].
Do not falsely [discriminate] between birth and death. Sentient beings are fundamentally unborn from the beginning; like illusory flowers, they ultimately do not arise.

Do not wait for them with cataracts; do not seek them through delusion. This is as explained below under the section on "empty flowers," where the metaphor has already been contained and interpreted. The text is easy to understand.

Below the section on "birth and death and nirvana," it means that when one is deluded, one perceives birth and death as if illusory flowers were arising; when one awakens, one attains what is like nirvana.
The flower ceases. To say that Perfect Enlightenment is free from flowers and free from cataracts is to sweep away birth and death.
Good son, you should know that empty space is neither temporarily existent nor temporarily non-existent;

how much more so for the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, which accords with it and constitutes the equal, fundamental nature of empty space? It is like refining gold ore: the gold does not come into existence through the refining. Once—
Once it has become gold, it is not again treated as ore; even after an infinite amount of time, the nature of the gold does not perish.
One should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is likewise so.

Regarding those who awaken to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the *Buddhottama-sūtra* states: "Emptiness arises within great awakening," and further says: "Quiescent illumination contains the void. It further speaks of "equality" (*samatā*).
Although Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is the nature of the void, it is darkly merged and undivided, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
It is without distinction or limit, and there is no differentiation between that which relies and that upon which it relies; therefore, it is called "equal. This is the intended meaning.
Emptiness resides within awakening; emptiness tends toward eternal quiescence. How much more so when awakening realizes the nature of emptiness—how could there be increase or decrease?
Even a metaphor cannot fully capture this, hence the phrase "how much more so" (況復) in the subsequent text. The later passage concerning the analogy of gold ore answers the third objection.

Mount Shān said: "These words concern empty space and worldly phenomena; they do not even share the same arising and ceasing as flowers, let alone the Tathāgata who accords with Perfect Enlightenment—tranquil, true, and eternal.
Is he the very essence of empty space? The analogy of gold and ore means that gold exists within the ore;

when the ore is smelted, the gold appears, yet it does not come into being for the first time through the smelting. If it were to exist only because of the smelting, then one might as well smelt a piece of顽石 (hard stone)."

...and so forth. One should likewise obtain gold [from the ore]. Thus we know that although it must undergo the process of being placed in a furnace and melted down, the nature of gold must necessarily exist inherently.

Now that it has already become gold, the following clarifies that while gold was hidden within the ore, it becomes manifest once removed from the ore; though its states of concealment and manifestation differ, [the gold itself remains constant].
The nature of gold is fundamentally equal; one should not say that it was originally unaccomplished.

This is because ore is used as a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*), while gold is a metaphor for the enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*). When refined until it is pure, it then possesses brilliant luster.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is likewise so. The World-Honored One’s intention was also to say: although the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching is uniform, delusion...
Awakening does not preclude the formation of differences. Since there are habitual obstructions accumulated over many lifetimes, one must turn away from those habits to manifest the Truth.
Once the Truth is manifested, one attains ultimate purity.
Good son, within the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is fundamentally no such thing as bodhi or nirvāṇa. Furthermore—
There is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it;
there is no deluded saṃsāra. (A supplementary note states: The two phrases "originally no bodhi" [and "no nirvāṇa"] sweep away the names of the general basis.
Because afflictions and birth-and-death are transformed, they are called "bodhi" and "nirvāṇa. As for their essence, who is not the truth? The names are obtained only due to delusion.)
As Mount said: "First, the awakened mind is established as the primary principle; only later are its traces swept away. This clarifies that it is not a state of annihilation.

It merely means being free from what is to be swept away; it does not mean the absence of the awakened mind, nor the absence of bodhi. Below, all instances involve sweeping away dualistic oppositions. Within Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue), none of these things exist at all.
If one perceives even the slightest [duality], one becomes deluded regarding Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Regarding phenomena..."
If there is seeing, this is not yet seeing. If there is no seeing, only then does one see the Buddha.

Son of good family, even the perfected sphere of the śrāvakas—in which body, mind, and speech are all utterly extinguished—cannot ultimately reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own direct realization; how much less could it be fathomed by a mind of discursive thought?
To attempt to cross the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly's glow; it can never succeed.
With a mind of saṃsāra, one gives rise to views of saṃsāra; such a person may enter the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, yet they can never reach its depths.

[Supplementary Note states: "The total cessation of body, mind, and speech is merely a state of stagnation in empty stillness. Those who attain the wisdom of the extinction of the meditative body can never reach Nirvana.

It is said that if one has not yet entered extinction, it is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana with remainder); if one has already entered extinction, it is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana without remainder).
Below, in the second section concerning the time of true awakening within the ordinary mind, there exists the thinking mind as a seed."
This refers to various forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "Taking fireflies to burn a mountain" is an illustration (used below to reveal the nature of mental afflictions).
As it says in the *Shanru* [Treatise]: "The true wisdom of the 'Lesser Sages' (*śrāvaka*) cannot yet personally reach the principle of the Lesser Sage;

how much less can the ordinary mind, which is inferior to that prior wisdom, reach True Awakening, which transcends that principle? Being separated by ever-increasing degrees of distance, how could it possibly create [it]?"

Yes. Just as the hundred officials still stand in awe of the Chancellor, how could the common people ever feel intimate with the Son of Heaven? This is precisely the same as in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
even those who have attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa path do not harbor the thought, "I have realized the four fruits.

How much less could the Tathāgata possess a fixed dharma by which he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Second, the raising of metaphors reveals the nature of mental states; these all manifest the discriminative mind. It is not...
This can realize awakening. It subtly satirizes the three preceding types by overturning their doubts and difficulties.

What was previously called "the mind of contemplation" is here termed "the mind of saṃsāra"; what was previously called "the realm of Perfect Enlightenment" is here termed "the great ocean of quiescent extinction.
One should reflect deeply upon this.
Therefore, I say that all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
(As the Mountain Master said: "This is to temporarily cease the deluded mind," referring to the preceding passage on not yet having emerged from saṃsāra.)

"Good son, there are those who engage in conceptualization arising from the mind; these are all merely the vaporous conditions of deluded thoughts regarding the six sense-objects, not the true essence of the mind, being like flowers in the sky.

To use such conceptualization to discern the realm of the Buddha is like taking flowers in the sky to further produce fruits in the sky—it is a case of revolving through deluded thoughts, and no such state exists."
(An appended note says: Some interpret "arising from the state of having mind" as referring to the root-consciousness that initiates [thought].
"Having mind" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); "arising" refers to mental factors (*caitta*). These are all the illusory conditions of the six sense-objects.
This refers to the objective realms that act as attractors; they are not the true essence of the mind, for it is said that the true mind is without thought).
Mount Shān said: "Even if these words were truly about the existence of discursive thought (*vitarka*), such thought still cannot realize awakening;

how much less so this mind, which has long been like a flower in the sky, lacking any inherent substance. To further seek realization above this—how is this any different from a flower in the sky bearing fruit?
Therefore, it is said that these are merely successive delusive thoughts."
"Good son, a false and floating mind, full of various clever views, cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.
Such discrimination is not a correct question."
(An added note says: The general purport of this major section is, in essence, to censure the faults of the questioner’s stagnant emotions and conceptual discrimination;
therefore, this [passage] is the most important contemplation therein.)
Shanran says: This is because of the doubts raised in the preceding three sections; it refers generally to the floating mind and clever views, which altogether fail to realize awakening.
The final two lines conclude that the questioning was not in accord with principle.
Appended is Master Lépǔ’s “Song of Floating Bubbles”:
Clouds in the sky, rain falls into the courtyard; upon the water, floating bubbles arise. The former has already ceased as the latter is born;
preceding and succeeding, they continue in an endless succession. Originally caused by drops of rain, the water forms bubbles; yet it is again dependent on the wind [to dissolve them].
Agitated bubbles return to the water; one does not realize that the nature of the bubble and the water are no different. Following along with their transformations, one takes them to be distinct.

On the outside they are bright and clear; on the inside they contain emptiness. Inside and out they are translucent like a precious pearl. Amidst the tranquil waves, when one looks at them, they seem to exist.
When movement and contact occur, they are again as if non-existent; the matters of existence, non-existence, motion, and stillness are difficult to clarify.
Within formlessness, there are forms and appearances; one only knows that bubbles emerge from within the water, but how could one know that the water also arises from the bubbles?

Temporarily using the analogy of bubbles and water for my own body—the five aggregates are a hollow collection, falsely establishing what is called a "person. Only when one understands that the aggregates are empty and the bubbles are unreal does one truly [awaken].
"One can clearly see the original reality.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to roam within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, how [should they proceed]?"
When shall the root of saṃsāra be severed? How many natures are there within all forms of saṃsāra? How many distinctions are there in cultivating the bodhi of a Buddha?
When returning to enter the midst of worldly toil, how many kinds of skillful means for teaching and transforming should be established to deliver all sentient beings?

(Maitreya—here translated as "The Kindly One" (*Maitreya*). "Kindly" is his clan name; his personal name is Ajita, which means "Unconquerable," because his supreme virtues surpass those of all others.
He is now addressed by his clan name, simply as Maitreya. Through this gateway, one deeply investigates the root of craving and sweeps away subtle delusions;
therefore, the cultivation and realization of the five natures all pertain to *saṃsāra*. Maitreya is [the Bodhisattva of] Equal Enlightenment.)

The Bodhisattva, in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha), manifests the elimination of even subtle afflictions and habitual tendencies, thereby immediately attaining the perfect clarity of Right Enlightenment.
As for the "Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction" (Mahāśāntinirvāṇa): it refers to the complete virtues of Mahāparinirvāṇa, which can carry forth the Great Meaning;
because its essence and function are profound and vast, it is likened to the ocean. As stated previously, one first severs the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
How should one now sever this? Previously it was said that all various acts of grasping and rejecting are samsara. I have not yet understood how many kinds of natures there are.

[The text continues with] "Cultivating the Buddha... and below, which asks about the cultivation of compassion, wisdom, and skillful means—namely, the vow to study boundless Dharma gates, which is to enter from the conventional into emptiness to achieve great wisdom; and because of the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings, it is to enter from...

Entering the provisional from within emptiness constitutes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Since the maladies of delusion are manifold, the prescriptions and medicines are likewise not of one kind. Without skillful means (*upāya*), it would be like adding ice to a small amount of hot water;
there is a fear that one might fall into the view of a recipient. Therefore, it is necessary to inquire.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Good son, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, have undergone saṃsāra because of various forms of affectionate attachment and craving. Thus it is with all the various natures of all worlds."
Whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation, all take birth through sexual desire. One should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root.
[Supplementary Note states: "Affectionate craving" refers to desire. Regarding "various kinds": these may be the affection of blood relation, such as that for parents;
or the affection arising from dependent circumstances, such as that for those one owes a debt to; or spontaneous affection, which is directed toward oneself and one's name.]
[Attachment to] profit, beauty, flavor, and one's six kin, or love arising from respect, love arising from kindness, or the binding of kindness through love—this is what is meant by "lust" (*kāma*).

It refers to being steeped in and attached to such things; it is simply a defilement of the emotions, and all such cases are collectively termed lust. Even in the case of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), it still depends on karmic defilement.
Mount Shoulu said: "The craving that is capable of grasping is the root of saṃsāra. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "The flowing of craving becomes the seed;
the reception of mental conceptions becomes the womb. Through their union, birth occurs; they attract those of similar karma.

By these causes and conditions, there is birth and death. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Because of craving, sorrow arises; because of craving, fear arises. If one is free from greedy craving, what cause for sorrow would there be?"
What is there to fear? Furthermore, the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states: "Where there is craving, there is birth; where craving is exhausted, there is cessation.

Thus, one knows that craving is the root of birth and death. As for the instruction to first sever it—just as one cuts at the root of a tree—it means that because of the five desires, craving is aroused, which causes sentient beings' cycle of birth and death to continue without end. [This applies to] all species in all worlds, such as those born from eggs...

The form of the moist-womb embryo is formed through the transmission of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of mental defilement; it is difficult to analyze in detail. Neither the nature of one's experience nor the destiny of one's life can exist without this.
Since both life and destiny are subject to lust, and lust in turn arises from craving, it is said that craving is the root.

Because various desires exist, they assist in the arousal of the nature of craving; therefore, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death. Desire arises from craving, and life exists because of desire.
Sentient beings cherish their lives, yet they still rely upon the root of desire. With craving for desire as the cause, craving for life becomes the fruit.
(The *Zhao lun* states: "The reason sentient beings have long wandered in saṃsāra is entirely due to their attachment to desire.
If desire ceases within the mind, then there will be no further birth and death. The spirit will dwell in profound stillness, its virtue merging with empty space;
this is called nirvāṇa.")
Zongmi said: "External sensory objects provoke the arising of affectionate desire; likewise, affectionate desire leads to attachment to those objects.
Because of this craving for desire, one creates karma; because of creating karma, one undergoes retribution. Thus, birth and death are not severed.
'Desire' refers to lustful craving; 'life' refers to physical life. Without affectionate desire, one is not born; without a body of desire, one does not exist. One should know this."
Desire exists because of craving; the body arises because of desire. Once this body exists, craving arises once more.

Because the body is produced by craving, it in turn becomes the cause for desire, further inducing the retribution of birth and death in the future. Thus, they revolve and continue in succession without end, giving rise to the various karmic retributions of the four [realms].
Due to the objects of desire, various favorable and unfavorable circumstances arise; turning their hearts away from love, they give rise to hatred and envy, thereby creating all manner of karma.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, they come to detest the path of karma and abandon evil to delight in goodness, thus reappearing as gods or humans.
(Zongmi said: "Various karmas" refers to the ten unwholesome actions and so forth. "Abandoning evil and delighting in good" means that one commits evil due to craving and desire;
since current desires are now to be loathed, one abandons the ten evils and delights in the ten virtues.)
As the Mountain said: "Because one craves those objects, when the objects do not accord with the mind, one gives rise to feverish distress and resentment. Due to resentment, anger arises;
due to anger, one commits killing, harming, and oppression, as well as beating, reviling, and insulting. All manner of evil karma thus originates from this.
Knowing that the mind of craving and desire is the cause of the evil realms, one should develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward those objects of desire and feel fear."
Those in the evil realms do not create the causes of evil; they develop a deep love and joy for the gateway of abandoning unwholesome dharmas.

Abandoning evil and delighting in good, they again manifest as devas or humans and obtain the retribution of happiness. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The ten paths of wholesome action are the cause for rebirth among humans and devas."

Furthermore, because one knows that all cravings are to be loathed, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Yet, this actually nourishes the root of craving, whereby there manifest the superior fruits of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*)—
the so-called "superior fruits" refer to the two realms' excellent retributions of both the primary and secondary bodies (*āśraya-vastu*).

Mount Shān said: "To know that both loving what one dislikes and loving what one likes cannot avoid suffering, yet to abandon that heart of attachment and take pleasure in cultivating the dharma of equanimity (*upekṣā*)—wherein the dharma of equanimity refers to the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis—while failing to realize that the mind which delights in equanimity is itself identical to that attachment, is why it is said that one 'further nourishes the root of attachment.
Because this concentration is cultivated and attained within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), each [level] corresponds to its respective stage."
And thus one is born in those heavens; therefore, they are called "superior fruits of merit.

Because these are all within saṃsāra, they do not constitute the Path of the Noble Ones (āryamārga). For this reason, sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death and avoid all cycles of saṃsāra [must seek the Noble Path].
First, sever covetous desire and eliminate craving and thirst.
(The Master Yuan’s *Treatise on Retribution* states: "Now, events arise necessarily from the mind, and retribution necessarily follows from events.
Therefore, by observing events through the lens of retribution, events can be transformed; by holding events up to scrutinize the mind, the mind can be reached. Craving...
This serves as a metaphor for its extreme urgency).
As it is said: "Since one knows that birth and death all arise from craving and attachment, if one wishes to escape birth and death, one must first sever craving and attachment."
Good son, all sentient beings, due to fundamental craving and the manifestation of ignorance, exhibit five distinct natures that are unequal;
these appear at varying depths according to two kinds of hindrances.
(*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Whatever is spoken of, it is established; all are called 'arising from the熏 [perfuming] of the teachings'"). Zongmi said:
"The aversion to evil and delight in good are the perfuming of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Once this habitual practice has become deep, it eventually forms a distinct nature."
If one encounters a false teacher, they will become extremely rigid in their attachment to the two selves of person and phenomena; this is termed "deep.

If one encounters those of the Two Vehicles who teach the principle of the emptiness of the person, although they have not yet abandoned delusion regarding phenomena, they no longer possess rigid attachment to the person;
compared to the former case, this is "shallow. If one encounters Bodhisattvas or Buddhas, the relative depth and shallowness can be understood by comparison.

What are the two obstacles? First is the obstacle of principle (*li-zhang*), which obstructs right knowledge and vision. Second is the obstacle of phenomena (*shi-zhang*), which perpetuates birth and death.
What are the five natures? Good son, if these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is said to be "not yet a Buddha."

(An added note states: This mind has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning. Because it does not realize the single Dharma-realm, thoughts suddenly arise in a manner dissociated from the mind;
this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the mind is defiled by ignorance, there is a "defiled mind.
The meaning of a "defiled mind" refers to that which is termed the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and so forth.)

Mount Shān said: "The obstacle of principle (*li-zhàng*) is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Because it fails to penetrate the nature and characteristics of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it obstructs the meaning of correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).

The obstacle of phenomena (*shi-zhàng*) consists of the six types of defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*), ranging from the three subtle states up to the arising of karma and the undergoing of retribution."

Because this [nature] has the meaning of continuing birth and death, one arouses the resolve, practices, and realizes [enlightenment] by means of severing the two obstacles; thus, the five natures are established.

Since this [nature] does not sever them at all, it is not included among the five categories. Furthermore, because one has neither yet aroused the resolve nor encountered the teaching, it is said to be "unperfumed."

If there are sentient beings who have completely abandoned craving and desire, and have first eliminated the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), yet have not severed the obstacles of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*),
they are only able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, but are not yet able to manifestly abide in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
(Zongmi says: "One knows the suffering of birth and death and brings the攀緣 (*pān-yuan*, objective attachments) to rest; therefore it is said that 'phenomenal things' are eliminated.

In reality, however, one has not yet been able to eliminate the three subtle [delusions]. (Supplementary Note says: "There are obstacles regarding phenomena and principle, and attachments regarding persons and dharmas. Now, one only severs the former.")
Therefore it is said: "One can only awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

As Mount Shān said: "If one does not first awaken to the Principle (li), but merely first eliminates phenomena (shi), one will consequently only be able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, yet remain unable to manifest and abide in the Buddha-realm. This is like a guest of the Elder who remains only at the rear.
He cleared away the refuse from the garden and took up residence in a grass hut, not yet daring to occupy the main hall.
"Good son, if all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the Great Perfect Enlightenment Ocean of the Tathāgata, they must first make vows and gradually sever all hindrances.
When the hindrances are exhausted and the vows fulfilled, they shall ascend the pure Dharma Palace of liberation and realize [enlightenment]."
The Realm of the Wondrous Adornment of Great Perfect Enlightenment.
(Supplementary Note: "The Realm of Wondrous Adornment" refers to the fulfillment of vows; when one encounters objects and conditions, all dharmas are none other than perfect enlightenment.
Hence it is called the Realm of Wondrous Adornment, meaning a domain.)
Mount Shān said: "Although the principle is realized all at once as emptiness, phenomena must be gradually eliminated before they are exhausted.

When the hindrances are exhausted, then throughout all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—whatever one encounters is nothing other than liberation; therefore, it is likened to the Pure Dharma Palace."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha,

saying: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, regarding all sentient beings, as well as the various bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones— what is the distinction between that which they realize and that which they attain?"
(Śuddhamati, this refers to practicing within this gateway; while amidst the characteristics of cause and effect in the realization of the stages (*bhūmi*), wisdom neither dwells nor clings.
With an empty mind, one forgets all marks (*nimitta*), remaining untainted by the characteristics of distinctions between practices and stages.)
Mount Shān said: "He raised the nature of awakening as it is realized to inquire about the virtues of the stage of the one who realizes it.
Since the single flavor of the awakened mind and the graduated distinctions of cause and effect are two meanings that are eternally divergent, it was necessary for him to pose this question."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati, saying: "Good son, the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is not a nature that exists as a nature;
it arises in accordance with all natures, yet is without grasping and without realization. Within the true mark (dharmatā), there are in reality no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings.
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations. Since these illusory transformations cease, there is nothing to grasp and nothing to realize."
[This section clarifies that Perfect Enlightenment has no realization. As the Mountain said: "Because the entire enlightened nature arises, the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases.
The *Dharmakāya-pravṛtti-pañcagati-nāma-sattva-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-body circulating through the five paths is called a sentient being."
Zongmi said: "Non-nature" refers to that which is not the five preceding natures, nor the nature of the various distinctions of saṃsāra such as craving and attachment.

"Nature exists" means that within those aforementioned distinct natures, there is universally present perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Perfect enlightenment does not abide in its own nature.
It follows conditions and pervades all differentiated natures. When these various natures arise, the entirety of the awakened nature arises;

there is no grasping and no realization, for it is said that this is not an object corresponding to the deluded mind. With respect to the presence of illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva; therefore, there is no grasping or realization.

However, regarding the previous cycle of saṃsāra and this present cultivation and realization, both are said to be "non-existent": the former is like the shifting of a shore, while the latter is like...
Regarding objective phenomena:
it is like the faculty of the eye, which cannot see itself. Its nature is inherently equal, yet there is no "equalizer" therein. Sentient beings are deluded and inverted;
unable to eliminate all illusory transformations, they manifest distinctions within the midst of their false efforts—efforts that are neither extinguished nor unextinguished.
If one attains accord with the Tathāgata’s quiescence, there is in reality neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent.

(Supplementary note: "In reality there is neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent" means that the nature of the mind is free from conceptual thought and is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.)
This is truly because ignorance deludes one’s own reality, stirring up discursive thoughts that cause the mind to undergo arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

From the subtle to the coarse, these states differ in their degree of intensity; they vary across the prior and subsequent limits. The prior limit is most subtle and is termed the characteristic of cessation.
The middle two or three [moments] are called the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*). The final stage is the coarsest, termed the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
Now, by the power of the熏 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of the inconceivable meaning of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeking.

Furthermore, through the perfuming of the teachings heard from the outflow of True Suchness (*tathatā*), these teachings perfume the original enlightenment, strengthening the power of innate understanding and diminishing the capacity of ignorance. Thus, one gradually approaches the source of the mind; first the characteristic of cessation subsides, and finally...
As his breathing ceased, he attained a clear and great awakening, realizing that the source of the mind is fundamentally unmoving.
As it is said: "The eye can see all things, yet it alone cannot see its own faculty.
Furthermore, when the light of the eye illuminates objects, the phenomena may differ in ten thousand ways, but the seeing itself is one; therefore, it is called 'equality. This is merely based on...
Regarding ordinary beings and sages, there is no mind that discriminates between superior and inferior; this is called the meaning of equality.
Furthermore, there is no one who can create equality. If sentient beings were free from delusion and perversion, there would be no sense of distinction.
One has not yet been able to eliminate all illusory transformations, meaning one clings to them as being real.

Regarding "extinguished" versus "not yet extinguished," this refers to the gradual exhaustion of obstructive habits, like a portion of dust being cleared away so that a portion of the objective field becomes clear.

Within the context of deluded effort, it means that upon the realization of perfect luminosity, one first comes to know that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent; thus, one perceives the functional power of the wisdom capable of severing them. Furthermore—
This is false and delusive; it thereby reveals the distinction [between the provisional and the ultimate]. This precisely marks the general designation of the stage of virtue.

"Tathāgata" refers to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), for all Buddhas have equally realized this principle. "In accordance with" means being in harmony with the fundamental [nature]; "conforming to" means being without contradiction.

It does not mean that one gives rise to a mind to seek quiescent extinction separately. In reality, there is neither quiescent extinction nor one who undergoes quiescent extinction; there is no subject and no object.
This means that when mental conceptions do not arise, one does not perceive any dharma of quiescence, nor is there any agent capable of quenching or causing things to become quiescent.
Good son, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been led astray by the deluded notion of a self and by those who cherish such a self. Never...
Not realizing for themselves that their thoughts arise and perish from moment to moment, they give rise to hatred and attachment, becoming immersed in the five desires.

If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the pure, perfect nature of *bodhi*, and they clearly discern the arising and ceasing of thoughts, they will immediately know that this very life is by its own nature a source of weary toil.

"Thought after thought arises and perishes. This refers to what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is like lightning; it does not abide for even a single moment of thought. The *Śāstra* states:
"All sentient beings are not called 'awakened' because, from the very beginning, their thoughts have continued in succession;

therefore, it is said that ignorance is without beginning. [Supplementary Note: To clarify arising and ceasing means that when one is deluded, it is precisely these delusive thoughts that arise and cease.
Because [the deluded mind] takes itself as the self, it does not perceive its own delusive thoughts, just as the eye cannot see itself.

Now that awakening has been attained, the mind is in profound accord with true enlightenment; therefore, one no longer takes delusive thoughts as the self, but uses the wisdom that accords with truth to illuminate thoughts as they arise and cease.
Mount Shān said: "My essence is fundamentally free from deluded thoughts. This is true for all beings within the four modes of birth and the nine categories of existence;
there is none who is not thus. The 'self' resulting from deluded thought is that which is grasped. Likewise, those who love me are also that which is grasped.

The view of self is originally non-existent; it exists only because of the mind. Since the mind is impermanent from moment to moment, the self also arises and perishes from moment to moment. This is due to grasping."

Because of me, those who follow me love me, while those who oppose me hate me; thus, they become attached to the five desires. If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to attain awakening, this is "external permeation" (*bāhyavāsanā*).
When the pure nature of *bodhi* is revealed, this is "internal permeation" (*antarvāsanā*). Wisdom shines forth brilliantly, manifesting the nature of the mind;
the delusive habits accumulated since beginningless time are suddenly awakened to and appear, just as one realizes a dream upon waking. Thus one knows.

At the time when the nature is deluded, that very nature gives rise to and ceases with delusive thoughts; it further exerts itself in toil and anxiety, devising thousands of schemes and ten thousand plans, with every thought never ceasing for a moment.

Furthermore, if there is a person who has eternally severed weariness and anxiety and attained the purity of the dharma-realm, yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstacle for themselves, they will lack mastery over Perfect Enlightenment.
This is called an ordinary person following along with the nature of enlightenment.

(An added note states: Regarding the purity of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): if it refers to the principle-dharma-realm, then within the essence of the dharma-realm, all wearisome concerns are severed and sensory objects do not arise;
this is termed "purity. If it refers to the phenomenal-dharma-realm, then the mind of discursive thought and concern...)
