The phenomena of differentiated sensory objects, such as the eighteen *dhātus* and so forth, should be regarded as non-arising;

this is termed "purity. As it is said: "Exertion and deliberation are forever severed; this is the mind that acts by transcending all signs. Whether the *dharmadhātu* is pure or defiled depends entirely upon one's own mind.
If the mind is defiled, it is defiled; if the mind is pure, it is pure. Regarding that state of purity, if the mind gives rise to attachment—
To give rise to purity within purity is called "pure understanding. Because the mind is bound to purity, it becomes an obstruction.

Since it is not disturbed by external objects, it is said to be "self-obstructed. Regarding the mark of realizing enlightenment, one directs the attention toward enlightenment; thus, one lacks mastery over Perfect Enlightenment.
To perceive that awakening differs from thought is to see that thought has no marks of difference; this is therefore called an ordinary person following along with the nature of enlightenment.

Good son, for all bodhisattvas, views constitute an obstruction. Although they have severed the obstruction of views, because they dwell in the awakening to those views, the awakening itself becomes an obstruction, and they lack mastery.
This is called the stage of a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the grounds, wherein they accord with the nature of awakening.
(An added note says: The preceding was named the "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*), which establishes the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). Second is the "stage of the worthy" (*ārya-bhūmi*):

the treatise entrusts its rest to the aspect of difference (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*), while this [present] is named the "bodhisattva," which establishes the stage of the worthy; the treatise entrusts its rest to the aspect of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*)).
Mountan said: "To see and understand constitutes an obstruction. This refers to the obstruction of pure understanding regarding what lies before one.

This identifies the characteristics of this stage by contrasting them with the preceding stages; it is precisely the awakening to divergent thoughts. Although the obstructions of understanding have been severed, the preceding stages still arise.
The phrase "though" prefigures that the subsequent thoughts are not different from the inferior [state] and so forth. Abiding in the perception of seeing is the mark of realizing awakening;
it is inferior to ascending the stages (bhūmi). Since that which is perceived is obstructed, the perceiving subject is likewise obstructed.

This is thus using obstruction to eliminate obstruction, and therefore lacks autonomy. This is called the Bodhisattva’s awakening to the stationing of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), wherein mindfulness has no abiding mark.
Good son, both illumination and awareness are equally termed obstructions. Therefore, the Bodhisattva constantly maintains awareness without dwelling [in it].
Illumination and the one who illuminates are simultaneously extinguished in stillness. It is like a person who severs his own head; once the head is severed, there is no one left to sever.
Thus, by means of an obstructing mind, one extinguishes all obstructions; once the obstructions are severed and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes the obstructions.
(An added note states: The three phrases, "constant awakening does not abide," clarify the characteristics of realization (*pramāṇa*). This means that through wisdom one realizes the principle;

wisdom and the principle are in profound accord, like the sun merging with space, or like a jewel illuminating itself. It is merely the manifestation of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*), for there is neither subject nor object.)

Zongmi said: "There is illumination" refers to the pure understanding within the stage of faith. "There is awakening" refers to the awakening that perceives obstacles within the stages of the worthy ones (*śaikṣa*).

Both are termed "obstacles," which precisely reveals the error of the former [stages]. "Constantly abiding in non-abiding awakening" means that illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescence;
this is the harmony between subject and object. Thus, there is no dwelling upon the mark of thought, and the dwelling upon marks is absent. It is as follows:
One takes a sword and severs one's own head. Before the head has fallen, there is no meaning of "one who can sever"; once the head has already fallen, there is likewise no person who can sever.

Thus, by using the awareness that perceives obstacles to extinguish the very obstacles that are perceived, the obstacles are severed and extinguished, yet there is no one who extinguishes those obstacles.
It is like fire emerging from wood: when the wood is exhausted, the smoke ceases and the ashes fly away.
The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; once one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
All the various verbal explanations of the Tathāgatas for the sake of instructing Bodhisattvas are likewise so.
This is called the Bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.

(Su Ziyou said: "It is like pointing a finger at the moon; this is the metaphor of the ancients regarding the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare. The Supplementary Note says: "This is called 'non-abiding instruction.

It means that before reaching the stages (*bhūmi*), one has not yet realized the True Principle and thus finds it difficult to forget verbal teachings. Upon reaching the stages and realizing the Principle, one does not dwell in names or phrases.
Because one does not dwell [in them], it is called 'true understanding of the teachings. Therefore, the text on the First Stage of the *Avataṃsaka* says: 'One attains the sūtras and śāstras...')"
As for the saying, "Mountains are like mountains": even if one speaks of words and images (*śabda-nimitta*) in order to grasp the intended meaning, there is no word or image that can cause delusion;

yet by clinging to words and images, one becomes confused about the Truth. Therefore, the finger pointing at the moon is used as a metaphor for verbal teaching, signifying that one must rely upon the finger in order to see the moon.
Section on the Ultimate. To awaken the mind, one must rely upon the Buddha’s teachings. It is like using a finger to point toward the moon: once the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten;

through the teachings, one realizes the mind, and once the mind is realized, the teachings are forgotten. To cling to the finger is to lose the true moon; to grasp at the teachings is to lose the fundamental mind.

The intention is to lead one to realize the truth and forget the signpost; therefore, it is said that "ultimately it is not the moon. From the phrase "All Tathāgatas" below, it clarifies that all Buddhas likewise [rely on this].

Words and expressions serve as a raft to reveal the principle. From the passage "This is called the Bodhisattva" onwards, the treatise finds its rest in the mark of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). The text states:

"When the stages of the Bodhisattva are exhausted and skillful means are perfected, there is a single thought-moment of correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*). One awakens to the initial arising of the mind; yet the mind has no mark of an initial state."
Because one is far removed from even subtle thoughts, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind; this mind is then eternally abiding, which is called ultimate awakening.
Good son, all obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening. Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation.
Whether dharmas are established or destroyed, they are all termed nirvana. Wisdom and folly are both universally identified as prajñā.
[Supplementary Note: "All obstacles" is the general heading. This means that when wisdom is luminous and perfect enlightenment (*圆觉*), there is no discriminating mind;
therefore, the ten pairs of dharmas listed below are all identical to reality—namely, the "seeing-nature as eternally abiding" and so forth mentioned in the treatise.
Following "attaining mindfulness," [the text] first speaks of the pair of consciousness and wisdom, second of the pair of establishing and refuting, and third of the pair of ignorance and wisdom.

Mount Shān said: "If one perceives that there are obstructions to be severed, then having severed them is called awakening; yet such awakening is not ultimate. Therefore, when obstruction itself is awakening, only then is it ultimate.
Regarding the two phrases 'attaining mindfulness' and 'losing mindfulness': if there is no-thought (*amanyana*), one attains right mindfulness;
if there is thought, it constitutes the loss of mindfulness. Thus, the treatise states: 'Awakening is the departure from thought; thought is [the state of] non-awakening.'"
Regarding "Awakening" and so forth: it is now clarified that mindfulness is fundamentally empty from the beginning and is originally non-mindfulness;

therefore, all are liberated. When various conditions assemble, it is called "formation"; when conditions disperse, it is called "destruction. Furthermore, advancing in cultivation is called "formation," while disparaging [the Dharma] is called "destruction.

Since conditions have no intrinsic nature, formation and destruction are of one suchness; thus, all are *nirvāṇa*. The two lines concerning "wisdom" and "ignorance" are from the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*.
As it is said: "Delusion arises from conceptual construction, yet conceptual construction itself does not exist. The nature of delusion and the Buddha-nature are equal and without distinction.
The dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are equally *bodhi*; ignorance and *tathatā* are not different realms."

All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are equally the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). Sentient beings and their lands share the same single dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands. Those with nature and those without nature alike achieve the Buddha-way. All afflictions...

Ultimate liberation. With the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, one illuminates and comprehends all phenomena as being like empty space; this is called the Tathāgata’s accordant awakening to the nature of reality.

(Supplementary Note: The three phrases concerning the Bodhisattva are to be read in connection with the preceding section as the fourth statement; it serves as a contrast between the heterodox and the orthodox.)
1. The opposition of the real and the false; 2. The opposition of defilement and purity; 3. The opposition of the primary [receptacle world] and the secondary [sentient beings];

4. The opposition of suffering and joy; 5. The opposition of having nature and lacking nature; 6. The opposition of bondage and liberation. (Zongmi said: The Tathāgata has realized this through the sudden forgetting of the mind.

Previously, he provisionally revealed various teaching gates according to the capacities of sentient beings, speaking of them as having depth and shallowness. Now, fearing that they might still harbor conceptual discrimination...)

Since there is no fixed time for awakening and entry [into reality], the "Perfect and Sudden Method for Settling the Mind" (*yuantun anxin*) is demonstrated. This accords with the realization of truth;

the former [method] follows phenomenal characteristics (*suxiang*), just as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra first explains the differentiated stages, positions, causes, and fruits, and subsequently integrates them through the equality of cause and fruit.
This is precisely the equality within differentiation and the differentiation within equality; the underlying intent here is exactly the same as that [of the verse].
(Li Zhou’s *Verses on Heaven and Hell* states: "If heaven does not exist, so be it; if it does exist, only the noble person shall ascend.")
If hell did not exist, it would be one thing; but since it does exist, the base person enters it.

As for the phrase "the dharmas that are accomplished," this refers to what is stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "One who abides in the Right Path does not discriminate between what is heterodox and what is orthodox.
As for the two phrases concerning "ignorance and *tathatā* (suchness)," this refers to what is stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "Ignorance..."

The primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*): its nature is fundamentally liberated. An ancient worthy said: "When deluded, suchness is false conceptualization; when awakened, false conceptualization is suchness.
These three phrases concerning the mindfulness of the precepts are precisely what the *Acaranga-sutra* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) states:
"Lust itself is the Way; wisdom and delusion are likewise so. Within these three matters, there lies the path of the Buddha who is free from dust. Sentient beings..."
The two lines refer to what is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "With my Buddha-eye, I survey the triple world;

all sentient and insentient beings, as well as all persons and phenomena, are entirely ultimate. "Ultimate" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). Regarding the two lines concerning the hells and celestial palaces:

it means that when extremely evil karma is completed, one sees the hells even within a celestial palace; and when extremely wholesome karma ripens, [one sees the celestial palaces] even within the hells.
This is precisely the celestial palace. The recollection of the two types of karma arises from the mind; how could the hells and celestial palaces be fixed?

Since the mind is fundamentally empty, all things are pure. Regarding the two phrases "having nature" and "lacking nature," that which is said to "have nature" refers to the nature of the Three Vehicles.
That which is called "absence of nature" refers to the nature of the icchantika. It is not merely that they will turn their minds toward enlightenment at some future time;
even now, they are already equal to those who have attained the Buddha-way. Regarding the two phrases concerning all afflictions, these are precisely what the *Buddha-śikhara Sūtra* states:

"The faculties and objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky. Since afflictions depend upon consciousness, and the nature of consciousness is empty, [afflictions are likewise empty].
As for what binds the afflictions, these correspond to the ten pairs mentioned above; although their names and forms differ, their underlying meaning is no different.

It is simply because one takes the Buddha’s realization of the awakened mind as the object, and that mind is free from grasping or rejecting, that one attains the universal, equal, perfect, and wondrous nature of all phenomena.
Therefore, I shall now merely cite examples for each and will not further investigate them one by one. "The ocean-like wisdom of the dharma-realm" means that the dharma-realm is profound and vast.

Therefore, it is like the ocean. Samudramati (Ocean Wisdom) is free from discursive thought; thus, all marks are like space. Furthermore, the wisdom that can illuminate is free from conceptualization, just like empty space.
This is identical to the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), who is like a mirror reflecting objects: the mirror itself has no mind.
Resting in awakening, one attains true compliance; therefore, one is called a Tathāgata.
Good son, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Do not attempt to extinguish the various deluded minds. Abiding within the realm of delusive thoughts, do not apply analytical knowledge.
Within this absence of analytical knowledge, do not discriminate what is real. When those sentient beings hear this...
This Dharma-gate: to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear—this is what is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.
(This passage consists of two parts. The section beginning with "However, those bodhisattvas... points to the method for settling the mind in the final age;

regarding the phrase "not understanding and failing to discern the true sentence," it is like the eye not seeing itself, and so forth. The section beginning with "Those various sentient beings... demonstrates entering the sudden [teaching] by relying on the Dharma.)
This refers to what is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*: "To be neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid—this is most rare. Mount Shān said:
"Distracted thoughts (*vikalpa*) are the grasping at and attachment to external phenomena. Since such thinking opposes awakening, one must cause them not to arise.
Yet, one does not extinguish or suppress these various deluded minds; for if one seeks the truth while abandoning the false, it is like discarding one's own shadow."
To labor the body while attempting to extinguish the false and preserve the true is like raising one's voice to stop an echo. For objects arise from the mind; they are originally one's own mind.

To add further cognition is to become deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, the Sūtra says that what is not illusion becomes illusion, and the Śāstra states that the mind does not see the mind, but simply does not give rise to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*);
naturally, it is like a mirror reflecting objects. Furthermore, the essence of the mind is fundamentally...
Awareness is already present; why must one further apply "knowing"? To initiate a cognition upon an existing cognition is what is meant by "applying.
When the capacity for knowing is stilled, that is true knowing. True knowing is itself knowing; who then knows the truth?

When those in the assembly of the root disciples hear this expedient means, their minds will be free from doubt. They will realize it with clarity, receive and uphold it, and thus peacefully accord with the Way.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, you have extensively analyzed for us such accordance with the nature of awakening, enabling all bodhisattvas..."
The luminosity of the awakened nature, by receiving the Buddha’s perfect voice, attains sublime benefit without depending on cultivation.
World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates; those who come from various directions do not follow only one path.

All bodhisattvas’ adornment of buddha-lands and their realization of bodhi likewise do not rely on a single expedient means. We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim this for our sake.
In total, how many kinds of gradual stages of all skillful means are there for practitioners,
which enable those who seek the Mahāyāna to swiftly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of nirvāṇa?

(Annotated note: "Majestic power and mastery" refers to the accomplishment of the three contemplations. Because their function is fierce and sharp, malevolent spirits cannot disturb them and delusive confusion cannot invade them.
Thus, through majesty and power, one leads the gradual realization of the preceding stages of reliance, as well as the sudden realization of forgetting the mind;

having obtained excellent benefit upon merely hearing this for a moment, one therefore requests it. There are two parts in the text: first, the inquiry regarding what is practiced; second, the explanation...)
As for what is meant:
the mountain says that the great city is a metaphor for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), and the four gates are metaphors for the various approaches to practice (*pratipad*).

Those who come from different directions do not follow only one path; for example, if one comes from the east, one cannot enter through the western gate. "All" and so forth refers to what was stated previously.
The explanation of active manifestation is clear in its principles; yet, as I now further inquire, I fear I may be overstepping my bounds.

Therefore, I first establish this reasoning and request that you respond according to my capacity. I only pray that you will deign to answer my questions regarding the practices to be cultivated and the person who cultivates them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying:

"Good son, the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades the ten directions and gives birth to the Tathāgatas. It is of the same essence as all phenomena and is equal. Regarding all practices, there is truly no duality;
yet the expedient means that accord with it are immeasurable in number. They perfectly encompass what is returned to, following the distinctions of individual natures."
There are three kinds.

(Supplementary note: "Identity and equality" refers to what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls "Buddha-nature" when it exists within the category of sentient beings, and "Dharma-nature" when it exists outside the category of sentient beings. (Supplementary note: "Skillful means and conformity")
Their number is immeasurable. This is what is meant in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "What is taught for one is not appropriate for another; for that person, it would be a false teaching.
Just as a skilled physician prescribes treatments according to each individual patient, so does the Tathāgata teach sentient beings according to their mental dispositions and capacities."

(An added note states: The three types of meanings are explained below as follows: 1. The contemplation of merging appearances to clarify the spirit; 2. The contemplation of giving rise to illusions to dissolve defilements; 3.
The contemplation of the numinous mind that transcends all dependencies.)
Zongmi said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions have realized and cultivated together that matter and mind are non-dual and that ordinary beings and sages are without distinction;
since they all rely upon the nature of awakening, they are equally identical. Regarding all practices, this is precisely the aforementioned gate of the two types of emptiness contemplation."

The faculties and their objects are universally purified; craving and attachment are both stilled. Compassion and wisdom function in tandem, free from signs and free from mind, always without anything to be attained.
No Bodhisattva is otherwise than this. Although there are differences according to specific circumstances, this underlying intent is non-dual.

Nevertheless, the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ—some are sharp, others dull; their afflictions vary in thickness, and their states of sinking or agitation are unequal. Accordingly, one follows their respective capacities and natures.
The teachings are manifold; otherwise, it would be difficult to enter them. Regarding the phrase "completely encompassing that to which they return":
although the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ in ten thousand ways, these three gates can fully include them all.

Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment and, with a mind of pure awakening, take stillness as their practice, they will, by clarifying all thoughts, perceive the agitation of consciousness.
As quiet wisdom arises, the adventitious dust of body and mind is forever extinguished.
They are then able to internally give rise to tranquil ease. Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions [are in harmony].
It manifests within, like a reflection in a mirror. This skillful means is called *śamatha*. (Supplementary Note:
"Taking up stillness" means not grasping at phenomena. When the mind first begins its cultivation, its power is still weak;
it is appropriate to take up stillness and remain composed, for only then can one extend the illumination. (Supplementary Note: Regarding "like a reflection in a mirror," a question asks: If all...)
The Buddha possesses spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-karman*) that can manifest in all places to benefit sentient beings.
Why is it that many in the world are unable to see this? The answer is: The Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is equal and pervasive in all places;

because it is devoid of volitional effort (*abhisamskāra*), it is called "spontaneous. It manifests solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. The mind of a sentient being is like a mirror. Just as a mirror...
If there are defilements, the physical form does not appear; likewise, if the minds of sentient beings have defilements, the Dharma-body does not appear.
The Sūtra speaks of the "Buddha-mind" and the Treatise speaks of the "Dharma-body"—mind and body are one, both referring to the fundamental source from which manifestation occurs.

If we were to speak in terms of what is manifested, it would be called the "response-transformation" (nirmāṇakāya). This is because when the mind is tranquil, it is known that the Buddha-mind is likewise so; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] manifests for them.
This does not mean that there is anything manifested within the Buddha-mind.
As the Mountain said: "This refers to the arousal of the mind and the practice of cultivation.

Desiring to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, one must first realize the pure, perfect, and enlightened nature within one's own body as the foundation of practice. To purify the awakened mind, one initiates practice based on what has been realized."
"Also. "Yi" (以) means "to employ. Ordinary beings employ delusion; Bodhisattvas employ awakening. Because delusion and awakening differ, they take stillness as their practice.
Although awakening is both movement and stillness, in order to provide an antidote amidst the turbulence of movement, they single-mindedly settle the mind upon the realm of stillness.
By practicing gradually in this way, they finally achieve success. This is because, by first using stillness to clarify the mind, all...

Thoughts do not arise; the mind merges with the source of stillness, and its essence is non-discriminative. Thus, when one perceives the consciousness of discrimination, it is vexed, agitated, and disturbed.

By means of the preceding thought’s clarification of the awakened nature, the nature of wisdom opens and becomes luminous. Because wisdom arises from stillness, it is called "still-wisdom" (*jinghui*).
This [wisdom] was hidden and is now manifest, hence it is called "arising. Through the arising of wisdom, the characteristics of body and mind are exhausted, and the delusions of sensory objects...
Non-arising is called eternal extinction; thus, the inner mind becomes naturally secluded, tranquil, pure, and empty. It is light, peaceful, and harmonious;
clamor and dust are forever stilled, and coarseness and heaviness are long dispelled. Now, the perfectly luminous essence of sentient beings is no different from that of the Buddhas;

it is only due to deluded emotions that the ordinary and the sagely appear separated. Now, as the characteristics of body and mind are exhausted and deluded thoughts do not arise, [the nature] is perfect.

The wondrous mind of enlightenment is where ordinary beings and sages interpenetrate. Speaking in terms of ultimate principle, I know that my own body and mind also manifest universally within the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions, just as various mirrors enter into a single mirror, whereby those various mirrors become reflected images.
Thus, the Buddhas enter the practitioner’s present mind like reflected images. However, the nature of a dusty mirror is fundamentally luminous; it must be polished and refined.
He then presented the Buddha image. The minds of sentient beings are likewise: when the mind is tranquil, the Tathāgata appears.

*Śamatha* is translated here as "stopping" (*zhi*); it is a synonym for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and carries the meaning of "quiescence. This refers to the fact that, regarding objects such as the defiled and the pure, the mind does not engage in false conceptualization.

"Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they use their pure enlightened mind to realize that the nature of the mind, as well as the sense organs and their objects, are all produced by illusion.
They then give rise to various illusions to eliminate those who are deluded; they transform these illusions to enlighten the assembly of deluded beings.
Because they give rise to these illusions, they are able to internally generate great compassion and ease. All bodhisattvas, from [this point]..."

This is the arising of practice. As it gradually progresses, the one who contemplates the illusion is not identical with the illusion; yet the contemplation of the illusion is not distinct from the illusion, for both are entirely illusory.
When one is forever detached from illusory appearances, this is the perfected and wondrous practice of all Bodhisattvas.
Like a sprout growing from the soil, this skillful means is called *samāpatti*.

(An appended note says: "To transform various illusions and open the way for illusory multitudes" means that, if explained through the contemplation of the mind, one gives rise to the differentiated wisdom of illusion and universally contemplates the eighty thousand hosts of afflictions (*kleśa*), seeing each as truly pure, neither obstructed nor obscured—this is what is meant by 'opening'.
(Zongmi says: "It is like soil growing sprouts; the seed is a metaphor for the awakened mind, and the soil is a metaphor for illusion.")

The Dharma is likened to sprouts, and illusory wisdom (*māyājñāna*) is the metaphor. This means that upon awakening to pure, perfect *bodhi*, one gives rise to illusory wisdom based on illusory phenomena;

from illusory wisdom, one forgets the mind and enters into awakening. Upon entering awakening, both of the preceding two [stages] are eliminated. (Supplementary Note: *Samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium-attainment.

Furthermore, "equal" (*samā*) refers to being even and balanced, because one is free from lethargy and agitation; "attainment" (*āpatti*) refers to reaching, meaning reaching a superior meditative concentration.)
Therefore, as previously stated, there is the "Illusion-like Samādhi.

As it is said: "The nature of the mind is consciousness; consciousness, together with the sense faculties and their objects, exists through the conjunction of these three, and thus is said to lack intrinsic nature."

However, ignorance arises from delusion regarding the Truth; therefore, it is called an illusion. These illusions are themselves illusory wisdom. "Illusion" refers here to fundamental ignorance, which is that which performs the illusioning.

To "eliminate the illusionist" means to rely on the power of the initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi), which is itself like an illusion, to partially awaken to and fundamentally eliminate non-awakening.
When the aspect of cessation is first extinguished and the aspect of arising is finally stilled, this constitutes the elimination of the illusion.

The two phrases concerning "transformations and various illusions" mean that, responding to the capacities of beings, one manifests transformations and preaches the Dharma to reveal to illusory sentient beings.
Because the sense organs and their objects have both dissolved, self and other are non-dual; thus, one can internally give rise to great compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*).
Since this compassion arises from emptiness and is not born of attachment or views, it is characterized by lightness, tranquility, and ease. From this, all Bodhisattvas [proceed].
Only through the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) can one give rise to compassion and wisdom, up to the fruit of Buddhahood. That which contemplates illusion is not itself identical to illusion;
thus, it sweeps away illusory phenomena (*dharmas*). Since that which contemplates illusion is not itself entirely illusory, it sweeps away illusory wisdom.

When the marks of illusion are forever transcended, one accomplishes the practice that is "non-illusion," which is designated as the True. It is like sowing grain and so forth: depending upon the soil, the sprouts grow.
When harvesting the seedlings, both the sprouts and the soil are discarded. *Samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium-attainment" (*dengzhi*);
among the various forms of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is so called because one is able to reach a superior state through it.
Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they employ this mind of pure awakening to neither grasp at illusory transformations nor at various states of stillness.
They clearly understand that both body and mind are hindrances; lacking the awareness of [inherent] luminosity, they do not rely on any obstacles.
Thus, they forever transcend the realms of both the obstructed and the unobstructed. When experiencing the world and their own bodies and minds, these forms remain within the dusty realm like—

Just as the sound from a hollow within a vessel resonates outward, so too do affliction and nirvana not obstruct one another. One is then able to inwardly give rise to the light ease of quiescent extinction (*śānti-praśrabdhi*).
This wondrous awakening accords with the realm of quiescent extinction, which neither one’s own nor others’ body and mind can reach.
The lives and spans of sentient beings are all but floating thoughts. This skillful means is called *dhyāna*.
[Supplementary Note: It is the luminosity of awakened clarity, the very essence of numinous wonder.
Yet this numinous mind has no crown above, no bottom below, no boundaries on the sides, and no location in the center. Since there is no "middle," how could there be east, west, up, or down?
If one wishes to call it empty and still, it is not like the vast void; if one wishes to speak of its characteristics and functions, they do not arise from conditions.
If one wishes to speak of its knowledge and vision, it differs from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). If one wishes to speak of its rigidity and obstruction, it differs from wood or stone.

If one wishes to speak of its awareness, it is not like the initial state of awakening from sleep. If one wishes to speak of its luminosity, it is not like the category of the sun or moon. Therefore, the various sūtras and teachings [state]:

Regarding the silence, emptiness, and non-existence, they are criticized as heterodox and petty; regarding the clarity of knowledge and vision, they mutually dissolve and mutually persist, each possessing a profound meaning.
(Zongmi said: "The resonance within a vessel"—here the vessel is used as a metaphor for the world, the body, and the mind; the sound is a metaphor for the numinous, luminous contemplative wisdom.
This means that because the sound emerges from the vessel, the vessel cannot confine it; thus the sound reaches far and wide, while the vessel remains localized.)
This location is used as a metaphor for contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which is cultivated through the body and mind; yet it cannot be confined by body or mind.

Contemplative wisdom is vast and boundless, while body and mind do not leave their original place. It is simply that the metaphor must correspond [to its meaning]; why dispute the substance upon which the metaphor relies?
Kuo said: "It is like a ten-thousand-jun bronze bell suspended in a star-pavilion; when the pestle is struck once, its sound vibrates throughout the entire universe. Shan said:
"By means of the mind of pure awakening, one treads upon that which is relied upon. Not grasping at illusory transformations is to depart from the second contemplation.
Reaching the point where all signs of stillness are transcended is to depart from the first contemplation. One thoroughly understands that both body and mind are entirely..."

This is delusion. The absence of conscious awareness and clarity refers precisely to the body and mind previously examined. Not relying on various obstructions, one directly attains the numinous clarity.
"Obstructions" refers to the aforementioned illusions that involve afflictions. "The unobstructed realm" refers to those who grasp at stillness as being identical to nirvana;
"the marks remain" means they do not differ from the ordinary. "The realm of dust" means they have not departed from their former location.
This arises from clinging to the identity of one's own substance with others; now that such sentiments no longer arise, how could they constrain the numinous illumination?

It is like the resonant sound of a golden vessel issuing forth without being obstructed by anything external. Internally, there is the emergence of quiescence, which means not grasping at illusory transformations.

Illusory transformations are themselves quiescent. One does not grasp at the mark of stillness; that mark of stillness itself is extinction. It is not that one intentionally quiets or extinguishes them.

Furthermore, this is simply the true mind and the ultimate principle; it is not a stillness that exists in opposition to illusion. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Quiescent extinction is called the One Mind.
This is not a stillness that results from the cessation of movement, nor is it an extinction that occurs after arising. Therefore, it is said: "Internally arising and conforming to the wondrous."
Awakening to quiescence means that at the time of contemplation, one’s mind accords with that of the Buddha; therefore, it cannot be reached by the body or mind of oneself or others.
This means that it is clearly understood only by oneself alone, while others do not see it, and thus others cannot reach it.
Even the capacity of one's own consciousness cannot construct it, just as a firefly attempting to burn Mount Sumeru. One must depart from emotional attachments to accord with it.

Therefore, it does not reach [the ultimate]. Furthermore, wisdom arises based on the substance; that which is produced by one's own sense organs and objects to give rise to consciousness is called "other.
Since consciousness cannot cognize wisdom, it fails to reach it in all respects. To thoroughly understand true quiescence is to know that sentient beings are ultimately not real;
this is termed *dhyāna*. This is translated as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). It is calm while contemplating; therefore, there is no distraction or movement. Thus...
It should be defined as being tranquil yet contemplative; therefore, it is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It carries the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vibhūticandra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, such a Dharma-gate is truly rare. World-Honored One, these skillful means [are for] all bodhisattvas..."
Within the gateway of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), how many modes of cultivation are there?

(Supplementary Note: The Buddha, through the medium of Bhadrapāla, accords with the myriad classes of beings; although this gateway generally elucidates the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), they differ according to individual capacity as being either single or combined.
Thus, each of the twenty-five wheels attains realization and entry. This Bodhisattva is well able to discern [these distinctions].)
[Answer: It is distinct. [The Buddha] possesses the perfect voice that adapts to all types; thus, he answers according to the question.
Zongmi said: "These various skillful means refer to the aforementioned three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

Although the preceding explanation of the three contemplations clarifies their respective characteristics, it remains uncertain whether the practice cultivated by the various Bodhisattvas consists of one person possessing all three, or whether three separate persons [each possess one]."
First: Is it sequential, simultaneous, according to order, or by skipping? For this reason, he asks.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇaruta, saying: "Good son, the perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas is pure and fundamentally has no cultivation, nor any cultivator. All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon..."
When one cultivates through the illusory power of the final awakening, there then arise twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
(As the Mountain Master said: "Wheel" (*cakra*) has the meaning of crushing and grinding; because it can crush the obstacles of delusion and cause right wisdom to revolve, it is called a wheel.)

Zongmi said: "Visualize a net with its meshes interlaced; within it, there are first three wheels for practicing the three contemplations individually, followed by twenty-one wheels for practicing the three contemplations in combination, and finally one wheel for practicing the three contemplations in their totality.
For these twenty-five contemplations, names have been established based on metaphors, each of which I shall now employ in full."
If a bodhisattva grasps only extreme tranquility and, by the power of that tranquility,
forever severs the afflictions and achieves ultimate perfection such that they enter nirvana without rising from their seat, this bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha alone.

(An appended note states: This refers to the contemplation of clarifying the turbid and ceasing activity. The fact that all three contemplations are marked with "only" (*wei*) and concluded with "single" (*dan*) is intended to show that they do not involve the other two;
it means that one's power does not encompass them, not that other practices are disparaged).
Mount Shān said: "One should only take up ultimate stillness and not engage in other activities. Through the power of a still mind, one realizes that body and mind are empty;
when even a fleeting thought does not exist, what basis is there for afflictions? When afflictions do not arise, this is itself the awakened mind;
therefore, it is called 'ultimate accomplishment. 'Without rising from one's seat' means not rising from the seat of the emptiness of dharmas, and thereby entering nirvāṇa."
This refers to entering into the nirvana of quiescence.
However, if bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, they may, through the power of the Buddha, manifest various activities within transformed worlds.
Fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva, he does not lose his tranquil mindfulness or various still wisdoms regarding dhāraṇī.
This bodhisattva is said to practice samāpatti alone.
(An added note states: This refers to the "Observation of Cook Ding’s Mastery of the Knife. Cook Ding used a single blade to dismember oxen, yet after nineteen years his edge remained unimpaired.

This serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva benefiting sentient beings and cultivating the myriad practices; though he enters the mundane world in response to conditions, his innate wisdom remains uninjured.)
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions and do not engage in activity, but instead sever afflictions alone,
such that when afflictions are completely severed they realize the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), these bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* alone.

[Supplementary Note: This refers to the contemplation of manifesting sound and transcending obstruction; it means that the physical substance and sound are fused, such that a resonance is produced in accordance with whatever strikes it.
(Zongmi says: Regarding these subsequent twenty-one contemplations, their sequence is discussed: first stillness, next illusion, and finally quiescence.)

Regarding the difference between *śānti* (quiescence) and *praśama* (tranquility): tranquility is the domain of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), while quiescence is the domain of the Buddha. Furthermore, tranquility refers to meditative concentration (*dhyānasamādhi*), whereas quiescence refers to nirvāṇa.
Within the text, there are three sets of seven: the first seven, the middle seven, and the final seven.
Mount Shan said: "Because illusory phenomena are boundless, it is difficult to exhaustively investigate them; therefore, one simply speaks of 'extinction. Extinction means the severance of thought.
Furthermore, since active engagement and purposeful action obstruct meditative stillness, one speaks of 'non-grasping. This alone decisively cuts off afflictions."
"Solitary" means not relying on any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). This is precisely the meaning of being beyond all dependencies.
When afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely severed, one simply accords with the numinous mind; the afflictions themselves become non-existent. This state of non-existence is itself the realization.

Subsequently, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are interwoven, with each contemplation serving as the primary focus while incorporating the other two. Thus, through this interweaving, seven [contemplations] are formed. Three.
Thus, there are twenty-one wheels; together with the three preceding single ones and the one subsequent complete wheel, they total twenty-five.
If Bodhisattvas first attain ultimate stillness and, with a mind of still wisdom, illuminate all illusory phenomena, then within that state—
One initiates the bodhisattva practice. This bodhisattva is said to first cultivate *śamatha* and subsequently cultivate *samāpatti*.

(A supplementary note states: "The former consists of the seven contemplations; this refers to the 'contemplation of the ferry that carries all across. When a bodhisattva cultivates concentration, emerging from the dust of the world is like the ferry;
when they develop wisdom to transform sentient beings, it is like carrying others across.)
Mount Shān said: "First, one takes the phrase 'ultimate stillness' as the primary objective, designating still contemplation as the foremost.
With a mind of still wisdom, one initiates the practice by following the traces of stillness. To 'illuminate all illusions' means to give rise to the practices of a bodhisattva within this state;

this is because one cultivates the contemplation of illusion concurrently. If one lacks still wisdom, one will remain mired within illusory transformations oneself; how then could one illuminate illusion?"
If a bodhisattva, by means of tranquil wisdom, realizes the nature of tranquility and thereby severs the afflictions, forever emerging from birth and death,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*.

(An added note says: This refers to the contemplation of the tranquil ocean and the clear sky. "Tranquil ocean" means the waves do not stir; one first employs still contemplation to reverse the flow [of consciousness].
"Clear sky" means the nature of water is lucid and pure; one subsequently employs silent contemplation to manifest this nature.)

Mount Shan said: "Because of stillness-wisdom (*śamatha-prajñā*), there is 'stillness' (*śama*). To realize the nature of ultimate stillness is 'tranquility' (*sama*). One treads upon stillness while concurrently cultivating tranquility.
As for the function of these two contemplations: severing afflictions is the extinction of the cause; escaping birth and death is the loss of the fruit."
If a bodhisattva, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifests various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings,
and subsequently cuts off afflictions to enter into cessation— this bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *śamatha*,
then practiced *samāpatti*, and finally practiced *dhyāna*.

(An added note states: This refers to the contemplation of the three eyes of Maheśvara. It means that all three contemplations are practiced together, just as there are three eyes on the face of Maheśvara.)
Mount Shān says: "By means of quiescent wisdom" refers to stillness. "Furthermore, manifesting below" means that after the illusory [activity], there is stillness.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate stillness, sever the afflictions and subsequently give rise to the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva.
He delivers all sentient beings. This bodhisattva is said to first practice *śamatha*, then practice *dhyāna* in the middle, and finally practice *samāpatti*.
(A supplementary note says: this refers to practicing the three points simultaneously. The "three points" are the Sanskrit letter *i*. My earnest intention is as follows:)
When a single person fully cultivates the three contemplations, this is called "simultaneous" (not meaning they occur at the same moment).

As Shan said: "By means of the power of ultimate stillness, there is stillness. Later he spoke of first attaining quiescence and subsequently [realizing] illusion; once afflictions are exhausted, [this state is attained].
Since attachment and views have already ceased, the conduct they initiate is neither impure nor unrefined; thus, one can untie the bonds of others.
If Bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate tranquility, sever the afflictions within their own minds and further deliver sentient beings, they establish the realm [of awakening].
This Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates *śamatha* and then practices both *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* simultaneously.
(A supplementary note states: this refers to the "single" and "double" contemplations. The former is the single, quiet contemplation, like the single mouth above;
the latter clarifies both stillness and illusion, like the two mouths below; hence it is called "single and double.")
Mount Shān said: "This refers to the integration of illusion and quiescence. Internally severing afflictions is quiescence; externally delivering sentient beings is illusion.

If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, empower and initiate transformations, and subsequently sever afflictions—such a bodhisattva [is one who integrates illusion and quiescence]."
This is called practicing *śamatha* and *samāpatti* simultaneously, followed by practicing *dhyāna*. (A supplementary note states:
This refers to a "single body with two heads" (*du-zu shuang-tou*). In the *Bai Ze Tu*, there is a mountain spirit whose head is like a drum with two faces, visible from both front and back.
This is a metaphor for the simultaneous illumination of stillness and illusion; the two function in equal harmony, like a double-headed [being].)
(Also, single, tranquil observation is like having only one foot).
As for "like a mountain," it means that by the power of ultimate stillness, one assists and triggers the power of transformation, thereby leveling the standards of both the tranquil and the illusory.

This means that by the power of ultimate stillness, one provides support and stimulates the power of transformation to deliver sentient beings, subsequently severing afflictions while simultaneously [accomplishing these ends].
It is quiescence (*śānti*). Because the former two [stages] are fully equipped with benefit for others, one enters the Middle Way; this differs from the former.

In the former, stillness and solitude constitute the beginning, while only later do they come to include both quiescence and illusion. Here, however, stillness and illusion are equalized at the outset, and only later does one begin to include quiescence alone.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, employ it to support quiescence and subsequently give rise to activity to transform worlds,
these bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha and dhyāna together first, and then practice samāpatti.

(An added note states: This speaks of the observation of the fruit falling and the flowers blooming. That is to say, by means of the tree of tranquil concentration, one binds the fruit of the Middle Way of quiescent extinction.

As for the subsequent blooming of flowers, it refers to entering the realm of sentient beings through the observation of illusion, delivering all living beings so that they may equally attain the fruit of nirvana.)
Mount Shan said: "To employ the power of ultimate stillness to assist in quiescent extinction is 'Equal Extinction' (qimi).
Subsequently, to exert function and transform the world is also 'Phenomenal Illusion' (huan)."
If bodhisattvas, by means of their power of transformation, accord with various conditions and thereby attain ultimate stillness,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti* and subsequently practiced *śamatha*.

(An appended note states: "In this sequence of the seven wheels, each begins with 'illusion' (*māyā*), followed by two others. This represents first the contemplation of the martial and subsequently the civil;
just as King Wu used arms to conquer Zhou but thereafter did not employ them, so too does this Bodhisattva first manifest various transformations and subsequently enter into quiet contemplation.")
Mount Shān said: "To manifest various forms through the power of transformation is to indicate 'illusion' (huàn).

To attain ultimate stillness while simultaneously embracing [the world] is 'stillness' (jìng). If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, attain nirvana amidst various realms, such bodhisattvas..."
This is called first practicing *samāpatti* and subsequently practicing *dhyāna*. (The supplementary note states:

This refers to the contemplation of "retiring from office after one's task is accomplished. When a Bodhisattva gives rise to wisdom to benefit sentient beings, this is precisely what it means for their task to be accomplished.)
To practice tranquility through internal cultivation is called "retirement from office.
As it is said: "The various realms produced by the power of transformation are like illusions; yet to attain cessation therein is 'simultaneous tranquility' (shānti)."
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, perform the work of a Buddha, abide in tranquil extinction, and sever the afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*.

(An added note states: This refers to the illusionist’s understanding of his art. First, he initiates transformations by performing magical feats; subsequently, because his essential nature is tranquil and still, he understands the art.)
Mount Shan said: "To perform Buddha-work through the power of transformation is illusion (*māyā*). To abide in tranquility is stillness (*śānti*).
To sever afflictions is serenity (*upaśama*)."
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions and abide in ultimate tranquility,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced samāpatti, then practiced dhyāna, and finally practiced śamatha.

(An added note states: This refers to the contemplation of the divine dragon hidden in the sea. It arises through the manifestation of illusory transformations, just as a divine dragon spreads clouds and rain;
it returns to its essential body and enters stillness, just as it hides in the sea.)
Mount Shan said: "To manifest through the power of transformation with unimpeded function is *huàn* (illusion). To sever afflictions is *jí* (quiescence).
To abide in ultimate stillness is *jìng* (tranquility)."
If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation and skillful means, reach tranquil extinction while remaining in accord with both,
such bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated *samāpatti* and are now practicing both *śamatha* and *dhyāna* in equal measure.
(An added note states: This refers to Nāgārjuna’s mastery of true contemplation—first manifesting illusions and subsequently returning to tranquil stillness.
It is like Nāgārjuna, who initially practiced illusory arts to extensively transform those on heterodox paths, and later cultivated the True Vehicle, personally attaining the fruit of sainthood.)

Mount Shan said: "To employ the power of transformation through skillful means is illusion (*māyā*). To accord with both ultimate stillness and extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is to incorporate stillness and extinction as well."
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, give rise to various functions to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever the afflictions,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice samāpatti and śamatha together, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna.
(An added note states: This refers to Śāṇakavāsin manifesting signs. Śāṇakavāsin was the teacher of Upagupta.
First, he manifested signs through his supernormal powers to subdue the arrogance of Upagupta’s disciples; subsequently, he entered meditative absorption and passed into parinirvāṇa.)
Mount Shan said: "To employ various transformative powers to support ultimate stillness is 'quiescence' (*ji*).
To subsequently sever afflictions is 'tranquility' (*jing*)."
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, supports their state of quiescence and subsequently dwells in pure,
effortless meditative concentration (*anābhoga-dhyāna*), this bodhisattva is said to practice samāpatti and dhyāna simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of śamatha.

(An added note states: This refers to the Great Penetration of Silent Contemplation. The Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū first employed transformative means to benefit sentient beings, and subsequently returned to quiescence.)
Mount Shan said: "To support quiescence with the power of transformation is to harmonize with cessation;
subsequently dwelling in pure, effortless meditative concentration is to encompass stillness."
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to supreme tranquility and abide in purity,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated śamatha.

(An added note states: These words clarify the contemplation of the ocean of reality-illumination (*bhūta-prakāśa-samudra*). The *Buddhapiṭaka-uṣṇīṣa-sūtra* says: "Together they enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s reality-illumination.

Here, the contemplation of the numinous mind is precisely the illumination of original enlightenment, which is "reality-illumination" (*yathā-bhūta-prakāśa*). Subsequent quiet contemplation is like the ocean of emptiness.)
Mount Shan said: "By the power of quiescence, one is 'quiescent' (ji). Yet, arising from that ultimate stillness, one abides in purity; this also includes 'stillness' (jing).
This corresponds to the following seven sections, which constitute the latter seven wheels (*cakra*). Each is headed by 'quiescence,' followed by the inclusion of the other two."
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence, give rise to functional activity such that their stillness and function are in accord with all objects,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.

(An added note says: This refers to the contemplation of the wondrous function of emptiness. The essence of the numinous mind is like empty space; its arising as transformation is the wondrous function. As Mount said:
"By the power of quiescence—this is 'quiescence' (ji)—one gives rise to functional activity within all objects; this is 'quiescent function' (jìng yòng)."
This conforms to [the previous point] and includes the illusory as well.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, settle various intrinsic natures in meditative concentration and then give rise to transformations.
This Bodhisattva first cultivates *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), then cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding), and finally cultivates *samāpatti* (attainment).
[The supplementary note states: This refers to the contemplation of the spirit of space (*ākāśa-devatā*). When this spirit encounters the reflection of sunlight, it briefly appears;
thus, there is first stillness, then tranquility, and finally the illusory.]
Mount Shan said: "By the power of quiescence, the various intrinsic natures are 'quiescent' (ji). To abide in meditative concentration is 'stillness' (jing).
To give rise to transformations is 'illusion' (huan)."
If a bodhisattva, by the power of cessation and through the unconditioned nature of things,
gives rise to the functioning of pure objects and returns to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this bodhisattva is said to first practice *dhyāna*, then practice *samāpatti*,
and finally practice *śamatha*.

(An added note states: This refers to Kāśyapa returning to meditative concentration—namely Mahākāśyapa. First he realized the essence, next he manifested supernatural powers, and finally he returned to meditative concentration.)
Mount Shan said: "By the power of quiescence and the nature of non-action, it is 'stillness' (ji). Arising as functional activity within the pure realm, it is 'illusion' (huan).
Returning to meditative concentration, it is 'tranquility' (jing)."
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence and through various forms of purity, abide in meditative concentration and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated dhyāna and to be practicing śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure.
(An added note states: These words refer to the mutual manifestation and observation [of the Buddhas]. The Buddha Prabhūtaratna first attained enlightenment and realized the essence of Suchness;
subsequently, from within his stupa, he initiated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is like the unimpeded nature of stillness and illusion.)

Mount Shan said: "To be variously pure through the power of quiescence is 'quiescence' (ji). To abide in meditative concentration (dhyāna) while giving rise to transformations is 'the union of stillness and illusion' (jing-huan)."
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), supports ultimate stillness and yet gives rise to transformative manifestations,
this bodhisattva is said to practice *dhyāna* and *śamatha* in equal measure before subsequently practicing *samāpatti*.

(An added note states: This refers to the manifestation through transformation from the lower direction; that is, the bodhisattvas of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, sixty thousand as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, appearing from the lower direction.)
Mount Shan said: "To employ the power of quiescent extinction (*śānti*) to support ultimate stillness is to harmonize with stillness; yet to give rise to transformations is to encompass illusion.
If bodhisattvas employ the power of quiescent extinction to support transformations, they give rise to ultimate stillness—the clarity and purity of the realm of wisdom."
This Bodhisattva is said to practice *dhyāna* and *samāpatti* simultaneously, followed by the practice of *śamatha*. (Supplementary Note:
This refers to the "Indranīla" [sapphire] which contains transformations and contemplations; this jewel contains all Buddha-images, and upon encounter, they manifest as transformations.)

They respond and then return to emptiness. Just as when the numinous mind achieves contemplation, it encompasses all virtues and functions; it responds to conditions by arising as illusion, yet remains tranquil and still.
As the Mountain Master said: "By means of the power of quiescent extinction, one aids transformation; this is to equalize with illusion, while giving rise to ultimate stillness and purity."
The wisdom that clarifies the objective realm is also accompanied by stillness.

If bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly integrate with all things, they remain inseparable from the nature of enlightenment regarding all characteristics and phenomena.
This Bodhisattva is said to have perfectly cultivated the three natures, achieving purity and accord.
(Supplementary note: In the final stage, one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations; this is called the "perfect cultivation of contemplation according to wish.

Like a wish-fulfilling jewel that illuminates all four directions, great wisdom is suddenly awakened, and the three manifestations are cultivated simultaneously. (Zongmi says: By means of perfection...)

Awakening encompasses all things; it is the arising of function from essence, wherein nature and characteristics are non-different. The nature of awakening is the convergence of function back into essence;
essence and function are unimpeded, and stillness and illumination are simultaneous. This is called the perfect, unsurpassed, wondrous awakening.
Mount Shān says: "It is because one gives rise to wisdom by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) in accordance with perfect enlightenment.

'Perfectly uniting all' means that the essence of all phenomena—such as the categories of reality and conventionality, principle and phenomenon, truth and falsehood, form and emptiness—are harmoniously integrated throughout their entire substance.

This is what is meant by 'perfectly uniting. It means that through the union of perfect enlightenment with principle, principle itself is no longer [merely] principle; therefore, it is entirely [that]."

Furthermore, because one unifies phenomena with awakening, phenomena are themselves no longer phenomena; thus, they are entirely identical to principle (*li*). The same applies to all other natures, characteristics, and so forth.
The meaning of the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is thereby manifested. Being neither principle nor phenomenon, it simultaneously negates both extremes to reveal the middle.

This simultaneous negation and illumination is what constitutes Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Moreover, based on various natures, one cultivates the contemplation of stillness (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); based on characteristics, one cultivates...

The Contemplation of Illusion. Because one cultivates the contemplation of stillness based on the nature of non-separation from awakening, the commentary states that this constitutes the "perfect cultivation of the three contemplations.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, if this awakened mind is pure by its very nature, for what reason is it defiled,

such that all sentient beings are bewildered and fail to enter into it? We only pray that you will reveal and awaken us to the Dharma-nature, so that this great assembly and the sentient beings of the future age may become eyes for the time to come."
[Supplementary Note: "Purifying all karmic obstructions" means that all karmic obstructions arise entirely based upon the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Through the questions and answers of this section, these are eliminated, and all karma naturally becomes pure. As Mount Shāna said: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the nature of all dharmas.

If translated literally as their fundamental essence, it is called the awakened nature (*bodhikṛta*); therefore, it is termed 'the dharma of awakening. If one investigates its various distinctions..."

All phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are identical in their single essence; this is termed "dharma-nature. Now, by analytically deconstructing the four marks and dissolving all phenomena into openness, they are entirely identical to the nature of awakening.
Mount Shān said: "The intent of this question is not to say that one is fundamentally and entirely deluded.

Rather, it clarifies that although one already knows the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) to be perfectly luminous and all phenomena to be pure, how is it that the ordinary mind remains as it is? It does not accord with the source of awakening;

whatever one does, emotions still involve hatred and love; self and others remain entirely distinct, making it difficult to achieve spontaneous integration. When compared to those who have realized the fruit, they are as different as heaven and earth."

The distance between them is vast. Since the awakened mind is fundamentally pure, if one were truly enlightened, it would necessarily be identical [to the Buddha's]. What further dharma could there be to defile it, such that my use of the mind would differ from that of the Buddha?
Therefore, it is said: "For what reason are you deluded and distressed, failing to enter?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, saying:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded by false imaginings and have clung to the existence of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life span.

They mistake the four inversions for a real self-substance. Because of this, they give rise to the two objects of aversion and attachment; thus, within a fundamentally illusory substance, they further cling to what is illusory."
(An added note states: The terms "self," "person," "sentient being," and "life-span" are four names given through successive shifts in meaning.
These four names, moreover, share a single characteristic: first, they are objects of deluded consciousness; second, they are objects of deluded wisdom.

The passage beginning with "All sentient beings" provides a general summary of these four characteristics as the causal basis for afflictions. The subsequent phrase "thereby" indicates that delusion gives rise to confusion.)
Mount Shān said: The World-Honored One taught that because sentient beings have never awakened, they engage in arbitrary conceptualizations within delusion;

they conceive of their own physical body as the self, and through the successive transmigration of this self, they take birth in other realms as humans, conceiving of the self’s prosperity and decline, its suffering and joy.

The various transformations of the continuity [of consciousness] are taken by sentient beings as a "self," and they reckon that the life-faculty of a single retribution remains uninterrupted as "longevity.
Now, the true self is fundamentally existent, yet through delusion it is said to be non-existent; the false self is fundamentally empty, yet through attachment it is taken to be existent.

All four are horizontal reckonings; therefore, they are called "perversions. Because one clings to these four characteristics as being the substance of a real self, one gives rise to attachment toward oneself and aversion toward others.
One loves those who accord with the self and hates those who oppose it. Such love and hatred both arise from clinging to a self;
hence it is said, "thereby," one further clings to what is fundamentally false by means of the false—namely, the four [characteristics].
The five great aggregates arise delusively from the nature of ignorance; being a mere provisional confluence of various conditions, they are already illusory.
Yet, upon this, one further clings to them as a self and a person.
Second, through mutual dependence on delusion, the path of deluded karma arises. Because there is deluded karma, one undergoes deluded transmigration.
Those who loathe this transmigration perceive a deluded nirvana; consequently, they are unable to enter pure awakening.

[Supplementary Note: Regarding the two lines on "the two delusions mutually depending," it means that karma is created due to afflictions (*kleśa*). The following two lines mean that retribution is summoned due to karma.

The final two lines mean turning away from the five destinies (*pañcagati*) and falling into the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). From this point, one gives rise to hatred and attachment, culminating in the false view of *nirvāṇa*.
This, in general, corresponds to the four truths of arising and ceasing (*utpādanirodha-catur-āryasatya*) within the doctrine of the Two Vehicles. That is to say, first...

The six phrases refer to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). The next two phrases refer to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The next one phrase refers to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
The final one phrase refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). As it is said: "Due to the two preceding delusions, one gives rise to and performs various deluded karmas.
Because karma can lead to the fruits of suffering and pleasure, it is called the 'path. Once karma is formed, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Birth and death...
"Transmigration" refers to the fruit that is reached. "One who is weary of transmigration" means being weary of the instability of the three realms, all of which are like a burning house;

it refers to ceasing conditions and severing delusions. To falsely perceive nirvana and set one's will upon entering quiescence—becoming addicted to emptiness by reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing wisdom—is precisely why such a person cannot enter pure awakening. This phrase is the direct answer that concludes the preceding section.

Question: The previous question asked why one becomes bewildered and fails to enter [the Way]. Now the answer states that it is because by clinging to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), one successively gives rise to faults;
even if one leaves the six realms of existence, one will again fall into the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). Thus it is.
It is not that awakening rejects those who are capable of entering; there are indeed those capable of entering, yet they do not enter through awakening.

Therefore, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought both lead to delusion and confusion. Why is this? Because from time immemorial, fundamental ignorance has existed as one's own sovereign master.

(An added note states: From the preceding passage, "Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening," up to "it is not because awakening enters [the mind]," these words express the delusion that rejects the awakened mind.
Therefore, the subsequent passage, "Thus, movement and stillness are both deluded," serves as the sentence regarding taking oneself as the sovereign;
it means that movement is my movement and stillness is my stillness. Since the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) is present, both movement and stillness are equally delusions.)
Mount Shān said: "The previous question asked why all sentient beings do not enter [enlightenment]. Therefore, the answer here states:
it is not that awakening rejects them and causes them not to enter; rather, they do not enter simply because they cling to a self, just as one whose dream-body has not yet been forgotten."

It is not that they fail to accord with one's own fundamental nature, nor is it that the fundamental nature rejects them. There are various modes of entry, yet these are not entries by means of cognitive awareness (*buddhi*).
The meaning is this: if entry were by means of cognitive awareness, then non-entry would constitute a rejection by awareness.

Since those who do enter are themselves engaged in the stages of faith, understanding, and practice, while the essence of awareness fundamentally has neither entering nor exiting, why should one hold awareness accountable for either entering or not entering?

Therefore, both the stirring of thought and the cessation of thought alike lead back to delusion and confusion. Now, since the stirring of thought constitutes a turning away from awakening, the cessation of thought should accord with the Truth;
why then are both called "delusion and confusion"? It is because they are both rooted in the beginningless *anādikālika-ālaya-avidyā* (fundamental ignorance residing in the ground).
It is for the sake of my Lord.
All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom; the nature of their body and mind is entirely ignorance. It is like a person who...
One does not take one's own life.
(The supplementary note says: Being born without the eye of wisdom is like a person who becomes blind at ten or twenty years of age;
although they cannot see objects before their eyes, they can understand them when described. However, if one is without eyes in the womb and is blind from birth, even when facing [objects],...)

When it comes to the nature of form (*rūpa*), though one may explain its various aspects, it ultimately provides no benefit. Therefore, one must first use a golden probe to pierce the film before pointing out what is right and wrong.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a blind person who does not know the color of milk; others may describe it for him."
Through successive metaphors—of a conch shell, rice, snow, and a crane—one ultimately cannot discern the color of the milk.
As it is said: "To be born without the eye of wisdom" means that one has never yet attained realization. Regarding the two phrases on the "nature of body and mind":
this refers to having previously attained the fundamental ground of the causal stage; thus, all that is cultivated is the cause of Buddhahood. This employs the fundamental origination.
Ignorance (*avidyā*). All of these are the works of Māra. Furthermore, previously, because awakening was perfectly bright, the faculties and their objects were universally purified;
it was concluded that "all is awakening. Now, since ignorance is the root, it is said that "all is ignorance.

The two lines beginning with "For example, there is a person" mean that one obtains a body due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); if one were to sever the body, it would contradict that craving. It is like a person... [text ends].
Even if one is base, wretched, or afflicted by illness, one still preserves one's own life and can never bring it to an end.
